places.chef: seafood counter, sushi · Kanazawa, Ishikawa · A tiny counter inside Kanazawa's historic Omicho Market, いきいき亭 has become one of the market's most beloved seafood-bowl stops, opening at 7am so visitors and locals alike can start the day with fish delivered straight from Kanazawa Port. With only about ten counter seats, the cramped space naturally turns strangers into companions over a meal. · Fresh fish straight from Kanazawa Port, served simply and affordably in a friendly, no-fuss market setting that's easy for solo diners to enter. · Signature kaisendon (seafood rice bowls) loaded with fresh local catch, including the popular Ikiikitei-don and the Tokusen Hokuriku-don (around 2,500 yen) and a smaller Mini Kanazawa-don (around 1,200 yen), plus per-plate nigiri sushi. In the Ikiikitei-don the fish toppings and the rice are served in separate vessels so you can eat them apart or combined.
places.gfd: This is a market seafood-bowl and sushi counter. Sushi rice is seasoned with rice vinegar and the bowls are served with soy sauce, which in Japan is virtually always brewed with wheat. There is no gluten-free menu or any documented allergen accommodation, and the cramped 10-seat counter shares all prep surfaces. Not suitable for celiacs.
places.vgd: The entire menu is built around raw fish delivered from Kanazawa Port (seafood bowls and nigiri sushi). There are no vegan or vegetarian options documented, and even the rice is served as part of seafood dishes. Not a viable choice for vegans or vegetarians.

places.notes: [Mom & Pop] Oden Takasago has been simmering its pot in Kanazawa's Katamachi district since 1936 (Showa 11), making it one of the city's long-standing old-guard oden houses. It has stayed in the same neighborhood, and its ivy-draped exterior, red lanterns and noren curtains give it an unmist
places.chef: owner/proprietor · Kanazawa, Katamachi · Oden Takasago has been simmering its pot in Kanazawa's Katamachi district since 1936 (Showa 11), making it one of the city's long-standing old-guard oden houses. Its founder had grown fond of Kanto-style oden while driving a taxi in Tokyo, which shaped the shop's unusually dark, rich dashi. Its ivy-draped exterior, red lanterns and noren curtains give it an unmistakably nostalgic Showa atmosphere. · Keep the founding broth alive by continuously replenishing it (tsugitashi), preserving a consistent, gently rich flavor across the decades. · Kanazawa oden in an unusually Kanto-style, darker and richer dashi — a continuously replenished broth topped up since the shop's founding. The slow-braised, melt-in-the-mouth beef tendon (gyusuji), skewered and served with the house's secret ginger-miso, is its signature. Other draws include seasonal kani-men (snow-crab oden, roughly November to December), whelk (baigai), kuruma-fu, akamaki and Kaga vegetables, plus less-common dishes like dote-yaki and curry oden. The ginger white-miso is also brushed over items such as daikon and tsumire.
places.gfd: Not celiac-safe. The defining dashi is built on dark soy sauce (wheat-containing) and bonito, classic ingredients include kuruma-fu (wheat gluten), and a ginger-miso topping is used. No gluten-free accommodation is documented.
places.vgd: A seafood-forward oden and izakaya house. The broth is a continuously replenished katsuo (bonito) and dark-soy dashi simmered with meat and fish, and signature items include beef tendon, crab, whelk and dote-yaki. No documented vegan menu, and even vegetable items share the animal-based pot.

places.chef: 髙野 幸 (Takano Sachi) · owner, chef · Higashiyama, Kanazawa — in the heart of the historic Higashi Chaya teahouse district. · A small home-style Japanese eatery tucked into the Higashi Chaya District near Sugawara Shrine, run by owner Takano Sachi, who carries on the hospitality her grandmother modeled. · The owner inherited her grandmother's belief that real hospitality is in genuine care rather than show — captured in the grandmother's words 'なんもないけど、ご飯食べて行きまっし！' ("Nothing fancy, but please come in and eat") and the idea that what truly matters is invisible. · Generous 'one soup, many sides' set meals built around local Ishikawa ingredients — a soup with several small dishes, plus a nodoguro (rosy seabass) set, served with carefully chosen Noto-area rice grown in Suzu (Koshihikari, Hitomebore, Hyakumangoku and other varieties) and local sake. Signature small plates include ikura shoyu-zuke (soy-marinated salmon roe), dried nodoguro, firefly squid pickles, and squid koji-zuke.

Wheat-based soy sauce and dashi are central to the menu and there is no documented gluten-free handling, so it is not celiac-safe. A traveler avoiding gluten would need to ask in detail and should not assume safety.

The space is a renovated roadside garage/warehouse, reimagined with high ceilings, moody lighting, mismatched sofas and curated art into what the owner wanted to be 'a cafe unlike anywhere else in Kanazawa' — a sophisticated hideaway that feels like the set of a foreign film. · Coffee-first craft (roasting and hand-drip done in-house) paired with an unhurried, welcoming atmosphere; the cafe is also dog-friendly, drawing friends catching up, remote workers and casual meetings alike. · Self-roasted specialty coffee is the heart of the shop: beans from various single origins are roasted in-house on a large roaster in the corner and hand-dripped to order, alongside playful drinks like tiramisu and prune lattes. places.chef: seafood izakaya / market eatery · Kanazawa, Ishikawa — inside Omicho Market · Omicho Shokudo has operated inside Kanazawa's historic Omicho Market since its founding in 1930 (Showa 5), making it a roughly 95-year-old market institution. places.vgd: A seafood-focused restaurant built around fresh fish bought daily at Omicho Market — signature dishes are seafood rice bowls, sashimi, and nodoguro. places.chef: oden shop, market food-court stall · 金沢 (Kanazawa, Omicho Market) · Ippukuya is a Kanazawa-oden stall set inside Ippuku Yokocho, a small food-court alley in the heart of Omicho Market, Kanazawa's centuries-old central market. The yokocho gathers a handful of stalls — Ippukuya for oden, a seafood/hamayaki grill stand, and a local-sake counter — under a shared eat-in space where you take a seat first and then order at each counter. · Built around the market itself — tofu items (yakidofu, atsuage, ganmodoki) come from the neighboring Tofuya Shibata and fish cakes from market kamaboko makers, so the oden showcases the produce of the surrounding stalls. · Kanazawa-style oden simmered in a gentle kombu-and-salt dashi. Signature and seasonal items include 車麩 (kuruma-fu, broth-soaked wheat gluten), ばい貝 (bay shellfish), and the local luxury 'men' pieces — のど黒面 (nodoguro), えび面 (shrimp) and the winter かに面 (crab) — alongside everyday oden like daikon, egg, atsuage, ganmodoki, octopus and beef tendon.
places.gfd: Not gluten-free safe. This is a Kanazawa oden shop whose dashi is soy-sauce/salt based and whose menu is built around wheat-containing items — the signature 車麩 (kuruma-fu) is literally wheat gluten, and fish cakes, atsuage and ganmodoki also typically contain wheat. All items simmer in a shared communal dashi pot, so cross-contamination is unavoidable. No dedicated gluten-free preparation.
places.vgd: Not vegan-friendly. The communal oden broth is a kombu-and-salt/soy dashi that almost certainly includes fish-derived dashi typical of Kanazawa oden, and the pot also simmers seafood (ばい貝 bay shellfish, fish cakes, のど黒/えび seafood items) and beef tendon. Plant items such as tofu, atsuage, ganmodoki, daikon and 車麩 exist but are cooked in the shared animal-based broth, so they are not vegan.

places.chef: Family-run Kaga cuisine restaurant, fishmonger lineage (Uo-goya Hanbei) · Kanazawa (Korinbo), Ishikawa · Gyohan traces its roots to a fish merchant house known as Uo-goya Hanbei that served the Matsusaka domain. places.chef: 村田 隆仁 (Murata Takahito) · owner, chef · 村田屋 is a respected, locally loved soba shop in the Moroe (諸江) area on Kanazawa's west side, run by owner-chef Murata Takahito. He sources whole domestic buckwheat directly from named producers, painstakingly hulls it, and stone-grinds only the amount needed for that day before hand-cutting the noodles. A handwritten sign at the entrance tells customers exactly where the day's buckwheat came from. · Freshness above all: buckwheat is milled only in the quantity needed each day, and the blend is adjusted depending on what producers and harvests are available, so the soba reflects the season and the best beans on hand, all at honest, reasonable prices. · Stone-ground, hand-cut soba (打たれる as 外一 / soto-ichi, a roughly 90/10 buckwheat-to-wheat blend, i.e. about ten parts buckwheat to one part wheat) served thin and fragrant. Menu highlights include the autumn-winter 鴨せいろ (duck seiro, ~1,580 yen) with a warm duck broth, the summer-only すだちそば (sudachi soba) topped with citrus rounds, and a 天せいろ (tempura seiro, ~1,620 yen).
places.gfd: Not gluten-free. The soba is made as 外一 (roughly 80% buckwheat, 20% wheat flour), so the noodles themselves contain wheat. places.chef: family-run yoshoku restaurant, longstanding neighborhood institution · Kanazawa, Higashi Chaya District · Restaurant Jiyuken is a Western-style yoshoku diner founded in 1909 (Meiji 42), standing right at the entrance of Kanazawa's Higashi Chaya geisha district. There is no gluten-free menu and no indication of allergy accommodation; not suitable for celiacs.
places.vgd: A meat-and-egg focused Western diner. The famous omurice is built on egg with beef and pork simmered for hours in a soy-based broth, and the menu centers on stews, cutlets and croquettes. No vegan options are documented.

It is widely described as the birthplace of Kanazawa's seafood-rice-bowl (kaisendon) culture, having begun serving kaisendon in the market from around 1989 (Heisei 1), and the long line that forms outside before opening has become a familiar daily sight in the market. · The shop greets diners in local Kanazawa dialect, conveying a warm market-stall welcome and inviting guests to try its many good things. · Generous kaisendon (seafood rice bowls) with more than 40 varieties available, from tourist-grade luxury bowls to sub-1,000-yen local options. No gluten-free menu, no dedicated fryer, and dashi/soy seasonings are used throughout. Not suitable for celiac diners.

places.chef: proprietor (店主), head chef (板長) · 近江町市場（金沢） · Located on the second floor of the Omicho Ichiba-kan building right inside Kanazawa's historic Omicho Market — the city's kitchen for some 300 years — Kofuku is a market restaurant that draws on the seafood stalls just below it. The proprietor sources fresh fish and shellfish such as crab, nodoguro (rosy seabass), oysters and sea urchin from the market each morning. · The kitchen emphasizes serving seasonal, market-fresh ingredients prepared to engage the five senses, paired with carefully selected local Ishikawa and Hokuriku sake. · The signature dish is a seafood hitsumabushi / 'sea treasure box' (海の宝石箱) eaten three ways: first as-is with a sesame sauce, then mixed with sea urchin, soy sauce and condiments, and finally as ochazuke with hot tea-broth poured over the rice. Other highlights include crab courses (かにづくし), seafood rice bowls (海鮮丼), and nodoguro served salt-grilled, as sushi or seared.

No gluten-free menu, allergen information, or accommodation is documented on the official site or other sources. Not suitable for celiac diners; you would need to confirm directly with staff and even then cross-contamination is likely.
places.vgd: The entire menu is centered on fresh seafood (crab, nodoguro, sea urchin, sashimi, hitsumabushi), dashi-based broths and miso. No vegan or vegetarian dishes are documented. Not a vegan-friendly destination; at most a plain side or rice could be requested, but this is unconfirmed.

places.chef: self-roaster, owner-operated kissaten · Kanazawa, near Omicho Market (十間町) · Higashide Coffee Ten is a beloved self-roast coffee shop just steps from Omicho Market in central Kanazawa, set in a red-brick building where the roasting machine sits proudly behind a glass front and the caramel aroma of roasting beans greets you at the door. It is a genuine retro kissaten, the kind of place where long-time local regulars have become part of the scenery. · An obsession with freshness: beans are ground and brewed to order, cups are warmed, and each coffee is poured slowly by hand at the counter so guests can watch and find the flavor profile they like best. · About 20 varieties of self-roasted coffee, from light to dark roasts, with beans hand-picked one by one to remove defects and sourced from Africa, Central and South America, the Caribbean and Asia. The signature Higashide Blend balances acidity and bitterness, and the famous house pudding (made with eggs, fresh cream, milk and vanilla beans) is a smooth custard that often sells out by evening. Souffle cheesecake is another homemade favorite.
places.gfd: A traditional self-roast coffee kissaten. There is no gluten-free menu or accommodation. The famous house pudding and the souffle cheesecake contain wheat/dairy/eggs and are made in a shared kitchen, so this is not a celiac-safe option. Coffee itself is naturally gluten-free, but no cross-contamination controls are documented.
places.vgd: The food offerings are limited to homemade desserts (custard pudding, souffle cheesecake) that contain eggs, fresh cream, milk and butter. There are no vegan dishes. Black coffee is plant-based, but milk/cream are served by default for milk drinks; ask for it black if you want a dairy-free drink.

places.chef: 金澤 忍 (Shinobu Kanazawa) · head chef (料理長) · Kanazawa, Omicho Market · Sushi Rekireki Omicho-ten sits right at the Omicho Market's Jukken-machi exit, just in front of Hokutetsu Kanazawa Station. It is the more approachable sister shop of 鮨 みつ川 (Sushi Mitsukawa), the Michelin-starred Edomae sushi restaurant in Higashiyama. The shop carries forward Mitsukawa's taste and technique while making top-quality sushi more accessible right inside the city's most famous market. · Drawing on the lineage of Mitsukawa, the kitchen applies careful Edomae preparation to bring out the natural texture and sweetness of each fish, sourcing ingredients daily from the local market and harbor. · Edomae-style nigiri made with akazu (red vinegar) rice — uncommon in Kanazawa — using fish bought daily from Omicho Market and nearby ports: flounder and horse mackerel from Nanao, scallops and abalone from Noto. The signature is the grilled nodoguro (blackthroat seaperch) hand roll, paired with lotus root and seaweed. The shop also pours an original-label sake brewed for it by Kanazawa's Fukumitsuya brewery.
places.gfd: This is a traditional Edomae sushi counter. Soy sauce (wheat-based) is used for nigiri, the akazu (red vinegar) rice and seasonings are not gluten-free, and items such as the grilled nodoguro hand roll and various preparations involve wheat-containing seasonings. There is no indication of gluten-free accommodation, dedicated equipment, or celiac-safe handling. Not suitable for celiacs.
places.vgd: A dedicated sushi restaurant built entirely around fresh fish and seafood from Nanao and Kanazawa ports and Omicho Market. The rice is seasoned with vinegar and the courses center on raw and grilled fish, shellfish and seafood. There are no documented vegan or vegetarian set menus; even rice and broth-based items rely on fish/dashi. Not a vegan destination.

places.chef: Hirata Kentaro (平田賢太郎) · chef-owner · Katamachi, central Kanazawa · Chef Hirata Kentaro opened Chikuwa's first location in the Katamachi nightlife district on August 8, 2015. The shop's name plays on the word 'wa' (輪 / harmony) — the idea of building connection and community over shared food. A second sister location later opened at Kanazawa Station (西口あんと). · Hirata emphasizes handcrafted dishes made fresh daily from seasonal market ingredients, with the belief that food should knit together warm relationships between people and their community, not just please the palate. · Kanazawa-style oden built around a 'drinkable' broth and house-made fish cakes. The dashi is drawn each day from Rishiri kombu and several kinds of dried fish/bonito, seasoned with Noto salt and local (Ono) soy sauce. The kitchen hand-makes its own chikuwa, hanpen and gobo fritters, with the chikuwa's mix-ins changing by season (citrus, Japanese pepper/sansho, Kaga vegetables). Creative twists round out the menu, like an egg topped with salmon roe, fried pork, cod-milt oden, and a mapo tofu with braised beef tendon and ground mountain pepper.

places.chef: Koichiro Koshikawa (越沢晃一郎) · owner · Kanazawa, Japan · Tsubomi opened in 2004 in the Kakinokibatake district near the 21st Century Museum of Art, founded by the long-established Kanazawa kaiseki ryotei Honami (穂濤). At the time, a ryotei operating a dedicated sweets shop was said to be the first attempt of its kind in Japan. The café grew out of the popularity of the kuzukiri dessert served at the parent restaurant, conceived as an approachable way to introduce guests to kaiseki culture. · Owner Koichiro Koshikawa describes the aim as serving the finest ingredients in the finest setting (最高の材料を、最高の場所で食べてもらうこと), personally visiting producers and selecting specific farms — for example a particular grower of Goroshima-kintoki sweet potatoes — rather than accepting any supplier. · Honkuzukiri — delicate, translucent arrowroot noodles made from the highest-grade Yoshino kudzu, served with kuromitsu black molasses — alongside honwarabimochi from premium bracken starch with kinako, white-dumpling cream anmitsu, kintoki sweet-potato zenzai, and limited summer kakigori such as the popular white-peach shaved ice. Every sweet comes with complimentary Kanazawa bocha roasted tea.
places.gfd: Several signature sweets are starch-based rather than wheat-based — honkuzukiri is made from premium Yoshino arrowroot (kudzu) starch and the honwarabimochi from bracken starch with kinako and kuromitsu — so they are inherently low in wheat. However, the kitchen documents no celiac-safe handling, no dedicated equipment, and items like anmitsu/zenzai and seasonal toppings may involve shared utensils or wheat-containing components. places.chef: confectioner, café · Kanazawa, Ishikawa, Japan · 和菓子 村上 was founded in Kanazawa in 1911 (Meiji 44) and has spent more than a century devoted to a single path of sweets-making. The Nagamachi shop in central Kanazawa sits near the historic samurai district, pairing a confectionery counter with a sit-down café (菓ふぇ MURAKAMI) where visitors can rest between sightseeing. · The house holds that 'the foundation of wagashi is delicious bean paste' (和菓子の基本は、美味しい餡づくりから), insisting on homemade filling and traditional technique carried on unchanged since its founding. · The signature ふくさ餅 wraps mochi and house-made bean paste in a soft baked skin; the black-sugar 黒糖ふくさ餅 is a classic Kanazawa souvenir. The eat-in café is also known for a honten-limited gold-leaf azuki soft serve, chestnut mont blanc, and seasonal wagashi such as 垣穂 (kinako and sesame) and the crystalline dry sweet わり氷.
places.gfd: Not gluten-free safe by default. While some wagashi are rice-based (mochi/anko), the signature ふくさ餅 has a soft baked skin made with wheat flour, and many traditional sweets and the café menu (mont blanc, soft serve) involve wheat and dairy. No celiac-safe protocols are documented; cross-contamination in a shared confectionery kitchen is likely. A traveler avoiding gluten would need to ask item-by-item and should not assume safety.
places.vgd: Some core wagashi (mochi with red bean paste, 黒糖ふくさ餅, わり氷) are plant-based by tradition, but ingredients are not labeled vegan and the eat-in menu includes dairy items (soft serve ice cream, mont blanc). No vegan certification or stated egg/dairy-free assurances are documented, so a vegan should confirm ingredients per item before ordering.

places.chef: family-run, long-established (since 1964), Kanazawa Oden 50-Year Veterans Association member · Kanazawa, Ishikawa · Amatsubo was founded in 1964 (Showa 39) in Kanazawa's Korinbo district by the current proprietor's parents, moving to Kakinokibata in 1984 and now run by the founders' son (the Amatsubo / 雨坪 family). places.chef: Masaki Otsuka · owner, chef · Kanazawa, Katamachi district · A brick-fronted Western-style diner (yoshoku) founded in 1957 by Taduzou Otsuka. It is now run by the third generation, Masaki Otsuka, who took over from his father and second-generation owner Shoji Otsuka. The restaurant is widely regarded as the most famous home of Kanazawa's local specialty, Hunton Rice. · Second-generation owner Shoji Otsuka held that 'diligently making delicious food matters most' (丁寧においしいものを作り続けることが大事), prioritizing quality and consistency over flash. · Hunton Rice — a plate of plain ketchup rice topped with silky, partly soft-set egg, fried marlin cutlets and fried shrimp, lavished with house tartar sauce and ketchup. No gluten-free menu, no dedicated fryer, and shared frying oil makes this unsafe for celiacs.

places.chef: kappo restaurant, Kaga cuisine · Kanazawa · A long-established kappo on Korinbo's Seseragi-dori, an area renowned as one of Kanazawa's culinary streets and within easy reach of the historic Nagamachi samurai district. places.chef: 手造り豆腐店（handmade tofu shop） · Kanazawa, Ishikawa · A small handmade tofu shop, founded roughly 40 years ago as a wholesale tofu maker, tucked into the historic Nishi Chaya geisha district near Nomachi. places.chef: confectioner, cafe · Kanazawa, Ishikawa · Rakugan Moroeya is a Kanazawa wagashi house founded in 1849 (Kaei 2, late Edo period), describing itself as having walked the same path as the city for over 170 years. In 2012 it opened the Nishichaya Karyo cafe, named Ajiwai, in the historic Nishi Chaya geisha district of Nomachi, combining a retail shop with a bright, welcoming tea space where travelers can shop and rest. · The house aims to honor the tradition of Kaga meika (famous Kaga sweets) and traditional manufacturing methods while continuing to refine flavors and products beloved in contemporary times. · Rakugan (pressed wasanbon-sugar candy) is the house specialty, alongside seasonal Japanese sweets, zenzai (sweet red-bean soup), kakigori (shaved ice) in the warmer months, and jonamagashi (premium fresh sweets). Signature confections include Hojo-gashi (方丈菓子), Kaga Hosho (加賀宝生), and Hana-usagi (花うさぎ).
places.gfd: No gluten-free program is documented. Rakugan is traditionally pressed rice-flour/wasanbon sugar candy and is often wheat-free, and zenzai (red bean soup) is rice-and-bean based, but namagashi (上生菓子) and seasonal items can contain wheat, and no allergen information or cross-contact controls are published. Celiac diners must ask about each specific item.
places.vgd: Traditional Kaga wagashi here (rakugan, zenzai, namagashi) are typically plant-based, made from rice, sugar (wasanbon/wasanbon-tou), and adzuki beans without dairy or egg, so vegan-suitable options likely exist. However, the shop publishes no vegan labeling and kakigori syrups/toppings and some namagashi may vary, so confirm ingredients per item before ordering.

places.chef: owner-chef · Kanazawa Saiya is an owner-run seasonal kaiseki restaurant a short walk from the east side of Kanazawa Station, working with fresh local fish, Kaga vegetables, and seasonal ingredients sourced from around Japan, paired with local sake from Ishikawa, Toyama and Fukui. · The owner emphasizes uncompromising, meticulous preparation paired with seasonal ingredients to create hospitality (妥協のない仕込みと旬の食材が織り成すおもてなし). · Its signature is Kaga jibuni served as a small individual hot pot (加賀治部煮小鍋仕立て). While the classic Kanazawa dish uses wheat-flour-coated duck or chicken with fu (wheat gluten) and root vegetables, this house makes its version with slow-braised pork belly (豚三枚肉) alongside Kaga nama-fu and root vegetables. Other seasonal dishes include white-soy-glazed eel, flounder-and-squash layered tempura, and seasonal rice cooked in clay pots.
places.gfd: Not gluten-free. The signature Kaga jibuni is made with wheat-flour-coated meat and Kanazawa fu (sudare-fu / nama-fu, which are wheat gluten), and the kaiseki menu relies on wheat-based soy sauce and dashi throughout. No gluten-free or allergy accommodations are mentioned anywhere. Celiac travelers should treat this as unsafe.
places.vgd: Not vegan or vegetarian-friendly. This is a seasonal Kaga kaiseki house centered on fish, eel, duck/chicken/pork, and seafood, with dashi-based broths throughout. No vegan or vegetarian menu is offered.

places.chef: Fujita (藤田) · owner, soba chef · Kanazawa, Teramachi district · Sobadokoro WAY opened in autumn 2024 on the corner of the Teramachi 1-chome intersection, inside a renovated building that previously housed a hair salon and a remake shop. places.chef: 木場谷光洋 (Mitsuhiro Kibatani) · owner-chef, itamae · Born 1973 in Toyama Prefecture; his family runs a fresh-fish business in Oyabe (Ishidō), giving him fish-sourcing in his blood. · After starting out as a salaryman, Kibatani found his calling working at a fish shop in Tokyo's Tsukiji market, which sparked a passion for seafood. He trained in Edomae technique at respected sushi houses including Yoshiura in Funabashi and the celebrated Sushi Aoki in Ginza, then spent years as a traveling (catering) sushi chef before opening his own counter, Sushi Kibatani, in Kanazawa's Hikosan-cho district in 2016. The 9-seat counter has since earned a Michelin one-star and become one of Kanazawa's hardest tables to book. · Kibatani speaks with gratitude about his hard years as a traveling chef and treats running his own place as a privilege, devoting himself to letting guests experience the full richness of the Hokuriku sea. places.chef: Japanese seasonal / kaiseki-style restaurant, part of the local MOMIJI GROUP · Kanazawa, Ishikawa · Ichirin occupies a renovated Kanazawa machiya on the Asano River in the historic Kazuemachi tea district, a townhouse that was the later-life residence of the American printmaker Clifton Karhu. The interior still displays pieces from his collection, so diners eat surrounded by his artwork while taking in the Edo-period atmosphere of the riverside teahouse quarter. · An emphasis on Kanazawa's seasonal local ingredients and regional sake, served in a setting that preserves the heritage of a Kazuemachi townhouse. · Seasonal multi-course Japanese cuisine built on local seafood and Kaga vegetables, paired with local Ishikawa sake; the kitchen is noted for being particular about its fish. Lunch sets such as the Hanakago box make the cuisine approachable at midday.

No dedicated fryer or allergen protocol is published; a celiac traveler would need to inquire directly in advance.

places.notes: [Mom & Pop] Uotsune is a family-run kappo set in a Taisho-era building on the embankment of the Asano River, just across from the Higashi Chaya District and near the Ume-no-hashi and Asanogawa-ohashi bridges. The weathered old structure is part of the draw: second-floor tatami rooms look out
places.chef: family-run kappo, Kaga regional cuisine, riverside counter and tatami dining · Kanazawa, Ishikawa (Kaga regional cooking) · Uotsune is a family-run kappo set in a building that keeps its Taisho-era character, on the embankment of the Asano River in Namikimachi, just across from the Kazuemachi and Higashi Chaya districts and near the Asanogawa-ohashi bridge. The weathered old structure is part of the draw: second-floor tatami rooms look out over the river, framing cherry blossoms in spring and colored leaves in autumn. · The house runs on a simple motto — 'oishikute yasui' (美味しく安く), delicious and affordable — pairing seasonal Kaga ingredients with the changing views of the Asano River. · Kaga local cuisine led by duck jibuni — duck simmered with sudare-fu wheat gluten and seasonal vegetables in a soy-and-mirin broth — alongside salt-grilled nodoguro (blackthroat seaperch), sashimi, and seasonal fish and vegetables.
places.gfd: Not gluten-free. This is a Kaga kappo built around dashi, soy sauce and seasonal fish. The signature jibuni is served with sudare-fu (wheat gluten) and a soy-and-mirin broth, and dishes use wheat-based soy sauce throughout. No dedicated gluten-free preparation. The kitchen does say it accepts allergy/dietary inquiries by direct phone, so a celiac diner would need to call ahead and discuss in detail — but it should not be considered celiac-safe.
places.vgd: Not suitable for vegans. The menu is centered on fish (nodoguro, sashimi) and duck (jibuni), and nearly everything is built on bonito/fish dashi. Vegetables are seasonal but prepared with animal-based broths and soy seasonings. The kitchen accepts allergy/dietary inquiries by phone, but there is no documented vegan offering.

places.chef: owner, soba chef · Opened March 1, 2022 in Kanazawa's Musashi-machi (Residence Musashi 1F), a short walk from Omicho Market, on the site of a former soba shop (元たんば屋 Tanbaya). · A casual hand-made soba house run by a welcoming female proprietor. The noodles are hand-cut daily using buckwheat flour from the Isoya region of Hokkaido, prized for its aroma and smooth, easy-to-eat texture, and the kitchen leans on local Ishikawa vegetables and seasonal ingredients. · The owner wants guests to enjoy the meal all the way through without tiring of it (最後まで飽きずに楽しんでほしい), which shapes the varied, lightly inventive menu; the duck seiro is even built to shift in flavor with yuzu and shiso as you eat. · The signature dish is tsuke-kamo seiro (duck seiro, ~1,800 yen): freshly hand-cut soba dipped in a warm, mellow broth built on Zao duck. Other standouts include a playful 'cheese soba' with Parmigiano-Reggiano and egg yolk (~1,300 yen) and bukkake oroshi soba with grated daikon (~1,000 yen).
places.gfd: This is a hand-made soba shop. The noodles are made with Hokkaido buckwheat flour but, as with virtually all Japanese soba, are not certified gluten-free and almost always contain wheat flour binder; broths and dipping sauces are soy-sauce based (wheat-containing). Not suitable for celiacs. No gluten-free accommodation is documented.
places.vgd: Menu centers on duck (Zao duck seiro), egg yolk, Parmigiano-Reggiano cheese, and seafood/vegetable tempura, with dashi- and soy-sauce-based broths. No vegan offerings are documented.

places.chef: Michihata (道端) · owner, soba chef · Kanazawa (Higashiyama), Ishikawa · Buemon occupies a renovated townhouse in a back alley of Kanazawa's Higashi Chaya geisha district. The building was once the private residence of the proprietor of 'Toyu' (東湯), a public bathhouse that the district's geisha once frequented. It has been modernized while keeping the chic character of the chaya district, with an open counter for solo diners and a courtyard garden visible through large glass windows. · A focus on hometown ingredients and Kanazawa's food culture, expressed through the marriage of soba with local Kaga roasted tea. · Hand-made soba, with the signature 'Kaga-bocha soba' (加賀棒茶そば, around 880 yen) made by kneading powdered Kaga roasted tea into fine sarashina-flour noodles (the flour deliberately mutes the soba aroma to let the roasted-tea fragrance come through); it is recommended eaten first with Noto salt. By day it is a soba cafe; in the evening it runs as a soba bar (音ゆ).
places.gfd: Not gluten-free. Soba noodles here are made with sarashina (refined buckwheat) flour blended with wheat and roasted-tea powder, and soba is typically served with a wheat-based soy-sauce dashi tsuyu. No gluten-free menu or precautions are documented. Not safe for celiacs.

places.chef: cafe, kissaten, dessert · The name 金魚庵 (Kingyoan, 'goldfish retreat') is drawn from the goldfish that appears in Kanazawa-born novelist Muro Saisei's novel 蜜のあわれ (Mitsu no Aware); goldfish motifs are hidden throughout the interior like a treasure hunt, and hanging goldfish lamps mark the vermillion lattice entrance. · Kingyoan opened on September 9, 2022 inside a renovated Kanazawa machiya more than a century old, tucked just off the main lane of the Higashi Chaya District. The whole cafe is built as a 'time machine' back to Japan's Taisho era (1912-1926), when Western culture was first taking root: red carpets, a phonograph, a period refrigerator, stained glass and antique furnishings fill the rooms, and staff serve in kimono with frilly aprons. · The cafe recreates Meiji- and Taisho-era recipes and decor to let guests step back in time and experience the romance of early-modern Japan. · Signature items include cream soda served in goldfish-bowl-shaped glasses; the summer-only goldfish-bowl soda whose decorations mimic water plants and bubbles; Haikara Punch, a colorful jelly-and-fruit soda (~800 yen); a dense old-fashioned homemade pudding with strong egg flavor and bitter caram…
places.gfd: This is a classic kissaten built around hot cakes, homemade pudding and other flour-, egg- and dairy-based sweets, with no gluten-free menu or allergy program documented. The signature white hot cakes are wheat pancakes. Not suitable for celiac diners; there is no dedicated gluten-free preparation.
places.vgd: The menu centers on egg- and dairy-rich sweets (custard pudding with strong egg flavor, hot cakes with honey and butter, cream sodas with ice cream). No vegan options are documented. Some drinks such as plain coffee or the jelly/fruit punch may be incidentally plant-based, but you would need to ask; this is not a vegan-friendly destination.

places.chef: Itaru Ishiguro · owner-chef · Kanazawa, Ishikawa · Founded in 1988 in the Kakinokibatake quarter near Kanazawa's Katamachi district, Itaru grew from a neighborhood spot into what locals call one of Kanazawa's defining izakaya, holding its loyal regulars even as the Hokuriku Shinkansen's 2015 arrival brought a wave of visitors. · The restaurant builds its menu around top local ingredients — day-boat fish from Toyama's Shinminato and Noto, and Kaga vegetables such as Gorojima-kintoki sweet potato, kinjiso red amaranth, Kaga futo-kyuri cucumber, and Noto taro — with chefs cooking in full view of the counter so guests can watch the craft. · The signature is the kioke-mori otsukuri — a generous sashimi platter heaped in a wooden barrel with bold seasonal cuts of Sea-of-Japan fish. Salt-grilled nodoguro (blackthroat seaperch) is another must-order. Winter brings yopparai-gani (sake-marinated kobako crab) and kan-buri (cold-season yellowtail).
places.gfd: This is a classic Japanese izakaya built around soy sauce, miso, and bonito/kombu dashi, with sashimi served with wheat-based soy sauce and many fried items (tempura, fried white shrimp). There is no documented gluten-free menu or allergen handling, so it is not safe for celiacs.
places.vgd: The kitchen is centered on Sea-of-Japan seafood (sashimi platters, nodoguro, crab, yellowtail) with dashi and seafood used throughout. While some Kaga-vegetable dishes exist, they are typically prepared with dashi or other animal products, and there is no documented vegan menu.
places.hours: 17:30–23:30 (L.O. 23:00); closed Sundays (and the following Monday when Sunday is a national holiday)

places.n: 魚旨 (Uouma)
places.notes: [Mom & Pop] The owner comes from an established sushi-restaurant background and personally selects the fish, bringing a trained sushi craftsman's eye to a casual market counter in the heart of Omicho Market.
places.chef: owner, chef · The owner comes from an established (老舗) sushi-restaurant background and personally selects the fish, bringing a trained sushi craftsman's eye to a casual market counter in the heart of Omicho Market. · A committed local-production, local-consumption ethos: Oku-Noto Koshihikari rice cooked with Hakusan spring water, blended with pure rice vinegar from the old Tsurugi town, and finished with a house sushi soy sauce built on Kanazawa Ohno shoyu — rice, vinegar, water and soy sauce all sourced locally for a balanced bite. · The signature is the 魚旨丼 kaisendon (around 2,480 yen) piled with twelve different all-seafood toppings in thick-cut slices, served over mild, lightly-tart vinegared rice meant to bring out the natural sweetness of the fish. Hand-pressed nigiri of seasonal local fish and the owner's own tamagoyaki round out the menu.
places.gfd: Not gluten-free friendly. This is a sushi and seafood-bowl counter built around vinegared rice served with house sushi soy sauce (blended on a Kanazawa Ohno shoyu base), plus typical accompaniments like tamagoyaki — all wheat-containing. There is no documented gluten-free menu, no dedicated preparation, and no allergy program. Not safe for celiacs.
places.vgd: Not vegan-friendly. The entire concept is fresh local seafood — sashimi bowls and nigiri. The signature dish is a 12-topping all-seafood kaisendon. No plant-based options are documented.

places.chef: Yoshie Koshida (越田良枝) and her son Kōta (皓太) · proprietress / okami, son / next-generation cook · Kōrinbō, central Kanazawa · Yoshibou is a long-running Kanazawa oden shop in the Kōrinbō district. It first opened in 1957, and after the previous owner passed away the shop went quiet for a time before the family revived it, continuing an roughly 70-year legacy; today it is carried on by proprietress Yoshie Koshida together with her son Kōta (the third generation), who set a warm counter atmosphere favored by locals and people on work assignment in the city. · The kitchen measures the salinity of the broth daily and adjusts the seasoning to the weather and temperature, aiming for a stock with lingering, deep flavor. The cooking avoids chemical seasonings in favor of a gentle, ingredient-forward taste, and the shop is a member of the Kanazawa Oden veteran-shops association (金沢おでん老舗50年会). · Kanazawa-style oden simmered in a light, local dashi built on bonito, kombu, Kanazawa soy sauce, sake and salt. places.chef: owner · Korinbo Rakuya is a Kanazawa machiya (traditional townhouse) izakaya tucked into the central Korinbo district, where the weathered wooden architecture, tatami zashiki rooms and a serene inner garden give it the feel of an old Kanazawa merchant's home. It is one of the comparatively few local spots where you can order Kaga regional dishes individually rather than only as part of a set course. · The signature dish is jibuni (治部煮), the classic Kaga stew of wheat-flour-dusted duck simmered with Kanazawa's fu (wheat gluten) and seasonal vegetables in a glossy thickened broth, finished with a sharp dab of wasabi. Rakuya is noted for serving jibuni as an affordable single à-la-carte plate, alongside seasonal Hokuriku seafood and Kaga vegetables paired with local sake.

places.chef: independent owner-operated cafe · 金沢・東山（ひがし茶屋街） · A small, independent tea-and-sweets cafe that has quietly operated for over a decade (around 13 years as of the mid-2020s), set inside a renovated traditional townhouse (machiya) on the main street of Kanazawa's Higashi Chaya geisha district. The owners describe their aim simply: to keep the spirit of an old-fashioned kissaten (Japanese coffeehouse) alive, refining the craft day by day. · Doing the simple things carefully — grinding and brewing each cup of coffee by hand, and preserving the calm, unhurried feel of a classic neighborhood coffeehouse rather than chasing trends. · Cup-by-cup hand-brewed coffee and Viennese coffee; matcha and hojicha parfaits; cheesecake; zenzai (sweet red-bean soup); premium seasonal wagashi (上生菓子); and, in summer, around eight kinds of Japanese-style kakigori (shaved ice, ~900 yen) served with the ice and syrup separate so guests sweeten to taste.
places.gfd: This is a traditional sweets cafe whose menu centers on wheat- and dairy-based items: cheesecake, parfaits, Japanese confections (wagashi/上生菓子), and zenzai. There is no documented gluten-free menu, no dedicated preparation, and no allergen handling described. Not suitable for celiacs.
places.vgd: Plant-based options are not advertised. Plain matcha, hojicha, and brewed coffee/tea are likely vegan as drinks, but the sweets (parfaits, cheesecake, wagashi, zenzai) typically contain dairy, eggs, or refined ingredients. Kakigori syrups may be acceptable but ice/sweets are not verified vegan. A vegan diner would need to ask in person and limit to plain beverages.

places.chef: townhouse café, traditional sweets house · Kazuemachi, Kanazawa, Ishikawa · Tsuchiya occupies a wooden townhouse built in 1913 (Taisho 2) in Kazuemachi, one of Kanazawa's historic teahouse districts, on the banks of the Asano River between the Asanogawa-ohashi and Nakano-bashi bridges. The building is a Kanazawa-registered traditional structure, recognizable by its deep red bengara-pigment walls. It has been converted into a small café that keeps the spirit of the old chaya intact. · A quiet, gracious tea-time: guests are welcomed with complimentary tea and a seasonal sweet while their order is prepared, and the second-floor tatami room is dressed with seasonal hanging scrolls and alcove crafts reflecting Kanazawa's four seasons. · House 'Tsuchiya coffee' (about 500 yen) and Vietnamese Dalat coffee, each accompanied by seasonal wagashi; seasonal specialties include wasanbon iced coffee in summer and zenzai (sweet red-bean soup) in winter, served on Wajima lacquerware.
places.gfd: Not a gluten-free destination. The café serves wagashi and toast-style items with no celiac protocols documented; the complimentary sweets are chosen by the house. No dedicated equipment or allergen handling is described, so it is not suitable for someone needing strict gluten avoidance.
places.vgd: No vegan menu is advertised. places.chef: 金沢おでん・おばんざいの居酒屋 · Katamachi, central Kanazawa · さんさん is a small, late-night oden-and-obanzai izakaya on the third floor of a building in Katamachi, the heart of Kanazawa's Korinbo-Katamachi nightlife district. A relatively recent arrival to the scene, it sets out to offer 'local flavors and drinks enjoyed casually at a bar,' with counter seats designed so that solo guests can drop in comfortably. · A relaxed neighborhood spot pairing Kanazawa's home-cooking traditions with easygoing late-night drinking, welcoming everyone from solo diners to groups. · Kanazawa oden simmered in a regional broth (including local touches like 車麩 wheel-shaped wheat gluten and 赤巻き red-swirl kamaboko), a daily-changing platter of obanzai home-style side dishes built around seasonal ingredients, plus casual izakaya small plates. places.gfd: A Kanazawa oden and obanzai izakaya. The cuisine is built on dashi (typically fish/kelp/soy-based broth), soy sauce, and wheat-based ingredients — Kanazawa oden famously includes 車麩 (wheel-shaped wheat gluten) and many simmered items soaked in soy-flavored broth. There is no documented gluten-free menu, dedicated preparation, or allergen handling. Not suitable for celiacs.

places.chef: owner · Kanazawa, Nishi Chaya District (野町) · Salon de The Kawamura is the second-floor tea salon above 甘納豆かわむら (Amanatto Kawamura), a specialty shop in Kanazawa's Nishi Chaya geisha district devoted to amanatto — candied azuki and other beans — along with yokan and jelly confections. The salon was created so visitors can sit and savor the same carefully sourced ingredients freshly made on the premises, with large windows looking out over the historic Nishi Chaya streetscape. · The salon is conceived as a quiet, serene space (静寂なる空間) emphasizing freshly made sweets from carefully selected ingredients, with the bean as the protagonist of each dish. · Signature offerings include a Kawamura parfait layering the shop's red beans with matcha, Kaga bo-cha (hojicha), apricot, mascarpone and soy elements; warabi mochi made with genuine domestic bracken starch served with house-made kuromitsu from Hateruma Island (波照間島) black sugar; and seasonal kakigori such as a hojicha shaved ice with house-made red bean paste, plus a matcha version, alongside strawberry preparations that use local tofu shiratama from a neighborhood tofu maker.
places.gfd: Not a gluten-free destination. The menu centers on Japanese sweets; while items like warabi mochi (bracken starch) and amanatto (candied beans) can be naturally wheat-free, the café also serves wagashi and dessert items that may contain or be cross-contacted with wheat, and no gluten-free protocol is documented. A celiac visitor would need to ask carefully about each item.
places.vgd: Several plant-based-leaning sweets exist: warabi mochi served with kinako (soybean flour) and kuromitsu (black sugar syrup), amanatto (candied beans), yokan, and bean-based jellies and parfait layers are typically dairy-free. places.chef: 前多 学 (Manabu Maeda) · owner-chef · Ishikawa Prefecture (born 1980) · Chef Manabu Maeda trained for about ten years at the well-regarded kappo restaurant Takeshi (割烹たけし), where innovative Japanese cooking won over an aspiring Western-food cook, then worked at a fresh-fish shop to master fish and knife work before going independent and opening his own place in August 2018. The shop's name, 'Minna no Manabu' (everyone's Manabu), reflects its friendly, unpretentious spirit. · Showcase fresh local Kanazawa and Kaga ingredients in honest, well-crafted Japanese cooking at accessible prices, served in a relaxed, welcoming atmosphere rather than a formal high-end setting. · Daily-sourced sashimi platters with six or seven varieties of fish, salt-grilled nodoguro (rosy seabass), and a much-loved beef tendon stew — the overwhelming bestseller — simmered two to three hours in a salt-based broth; seasonal Kaga vegetables and winter kobako crab also feature.
places.gfd: A traditional Kanazawa washoku spot built around dashi, soy sauce, sake and fried/simmered dishes (e.g. crab cream croquette, beef tendon stew). No gluten-free menu or handling is documented, and wheat-based soy sauce is central to Japanese cooking here — not suitable for celiacs.
places.vgd: The menu centers on fresh fish (daily-sourced sashimi, nodoguro), seafood, and meat dishes, with dashi-based seasoning throughout. No vegan or vegetarian options are advertised; this is a seafood- and meat-forward Kaga washoku restaurant.

places.n: 甘納豆かわむら (Amanatto Kawamura)
places.notes: [Mom & Pop] Kawamura began as a wholesale bean and confectionery business in Kanazawa with a history said to stretch back roughly a century. The family opened this retail shop in the historic Nishi-Chaya geisha district in 2001, set in a traditional wooden machiya directly across from the di
places.chef: confectioner, wagashi specialist · Kanazawa, Ishikawa · Kawamura began as a wholesale bean and confectionery business in Kanazawa with a history said to stretch back roughly a century. The family opened this retail shop in the historic Nishi-Chaya geisha district in 2001, set in a traditional wooden machiya directly across from the district's old geisha registry office, and renovated it in November 2013. · Handcrafted quality using local, seasonal Kanazawa ingredients, served in a calm, serene setting, with sweets made without artificial colors or preservatives even at the cost of a short shelf life. · Amanatto (sugar-candied beans made without artificial coloring or preservatives), alongside yōkan, seasonal fruit jellies, strawberry daifuku, and the beloved shitatari-mochi, a sweet-bean filling wrapped in gyūhi mochi so tender it seems to drip, sold with just a three-day shelf life.
places.gfd: A traditional wagashi (Japanese confectionery) maker. Many sweets like daifuku and shitatari-mochi are made from glutinous rice (mochi/gyūhi) and azuki, which can be naturally wheat-free, but yōkan, sweet beans, jellies and shared kitchen equipment mean nothing is verified gluten-free. There is no celiac protocol; ask in person about specific items before ordering. Not a dedicated gluten-free destination.
places.vgd: The core products are plant-based by tradition: amanatto (sugar-candied beans), yōkan, bean-paste daifuku and fruit jellies are typically made from beans, sugar, agar and rice with no animal products. However, some confections and the 2F tea salon menu may use dairy, eggs or honey, and none of this is labeled vegan. Confirm individual items in person.

places.chef: 上田穣 (Jō Ueda) · owner, chef · Kanazawa (Hirosaka, near the 21st Century Museum) · Before opening Ageha, owner Jō Ueda spent some 40 years working at a kamaboko (fish-cake) maker that supplied traditional Japanese restaurants, rising to factory manager. After leaving, he opened this small counter shop to share what most people never taste — surimi and satsuma-age eaten the moment they are made. · Ueda wants diners to discover that fish cakes and satsuma-age are not the supermarket-processed versions they know — that freshly fried surimi is something exceptional, served light, fluffy, and at its peak the instant it leaves the fryer. · The hugely popular lunch 'Ageha Gozen' (around 1,500 yen) brings together sashimi, just-fried satsuma-age, and seasonal seafood manju (sea urchin tofu, clam, pumpkin, sweet shrimp and more), with rice and soup, often finished with a seafood-kimchi dashi chazuke. Dinner is reservation-only chef's courses of fish-paste and seafood dishes, including an occasional 'raw kamaboko' made from fresh fish cured about a week until it sets.
places.gfd: Not gluten-free friendly. The kitchen specializes in surimi (satsuma-age / fish cakes) and seafood manju, and serves sashimi with soy sauce — fried items and fish-paste products commonly contain wheat starch/flour and the soy sauce contains wheat. No gluten-free menu or celiac accommodation is documented. Not safe for celiacs.
places.vgd: Not vegan. This is a seafood and fish-paste specialist — sashimi, satsuma-age, seafood manju, and fish-based courses are the entire concept. No vegan options are documented.
places.hours: Lunch 11:30–until sold out (approx. 15:00); Dinner 18:00–22:00 (reservation only). Closed Mon, Tue, Wed; occasional irregular closures.

places.chef: family-run, three generations, sushi counter · Kanazawa, Namikimachi — at the foot of Umebashi Bridge along the Asano River, near the Higashi Chaya District · A neighborhood sushi shop founded about 68 years ago and run by the same family across three generations. The name 八郎 (Hachiro, literally 'eighth son') comes from the founding grandfather, who was the eighth of twelve siblings. Today the third-generation chef shapes the sushi, having trained at the well-regarded Taihei Sushi in Nonoichi; his father, the second generation, still works the counter beside him, and his mother handles the service. It keeps the easygoing, good-natured feel of an old-fashioned Showa-era sushi shop in a neighborhood that has otherwise modernized. · Showcasing fresh local (jimono) ingredients through skilled, unpretentious craftsmanship while welcoming guests with warm, family hospitality. · Omakase nigiri and sushi-and-sashimi assortments built on local Ishikawa, Kaga and Noto seafood — seasonal fish, crab, and yellowtail — paired with local sake.
places.gfd: Not gluten-free friendly. This is a traditional sushi counter where soy sauce (wheat-based) is used throughout, and dishes like sushi rice seasoning, dashi, and accompaniments commonly contain wheat or soy. No gluten-free accommodation is documented and there is no celiac-safe protocol. Not suitable for someone with celiac disease.
places.vgd: Not vegan-friendly. This is a seafood-focused sushi restaurant centered on local fish, crab, and yellowtail, with omakase courses built around raw and prepared seafood. No vegan options are documented.

It sits a short walk from Omicho Market, where the chef buys fish fresh each morning rather than
places.chef: Yoshikawa family (4th-generation head chef) · owner-chef, family-run · Kanazawa, with founding-family roots in the Kansai region · A family-run sushi shop in central Kanazawa's Hakuro-cho, founded around 70 years ago by the current owner's grandfather and now run by the fourth generation of the Yoshikawa family. It sits a short walk from Omicho Market, where the chef buys fish fresh each morning rather than in bulk, keeping the catch consistently fresh. · Buying fish daily from Omicho Market to ensure freshness, and offering approachable, affordable sushi that keeps both locals and travelers coming back across four generations. · Local Kanazawa fish platters and the value-priced Ichihan lunch set (nine pieces of nigiri plus a thin roll and miso soup for around 1,100 yen, weekday lunch only). A quiet specialty is the anago (sea eel), simmered and then flame-finished (aburi) for a fragrant crust. Reflecting the family's Kansai roots, the menu also includes battera and grilled-mackerel sushi, plus a choi-nomi tasting set (around 1,650 yen) with sashimi, grilled fish, pickles and soup.
places.gfd: This is a traditional sushi restaurant where dishes are served with regular Japanese soy sauce, which contains wheat. Nigiri, rolls, miso soup, and homemade sweet glazes (such as on the anago/sea eel) are not gluten-free, and there is no indication of gluten-free accommodation or a celiac-safe kitchen. Not suitable for those who must avoid gluten.
places.vgd: The menu is built entirely around fresh seafood sourced daily from Omicho Market — nigiri, sashimi, grilled fish, and seafood sets. There are no documented vegan or vegetarian dishes; dashi-based soup and fish are central to nearly everything served.

While presenting at a university hospital event she was struck by how many more people live with food allergies than she had imagined, and that experience inspired her to open a bakery that people with dietary restrictions could enjoy without worry. · Everything is made with 100% domestic rice flour and no wheat gluten, avoiding the seven mandatory allergen ingredients and additives such as thickeners, and leavened with house-made apple yeast so that people with allergies can eat more freely. places.notes: [Mom & Pop] Daidai opened on April 29, 2023 in Kanazawa's lively Katamachi district, just behind Korinbo Tokyu Square. The shop's whole concept is to serve the city's two great local specialties under one roof: Kanazawa curry and Hunton rice.
places.chef: Isao Shimabukuro · owner, chef · Katamachi, central Kanazawa · Daidai opened on April 29, 2023 in Kanazawa's lively Katamachi district, just behind Korinbo Tokyu Square. The shop's whole concept is to serve the city's two great local specialties under one roof: Kanazawa curry and Hunton rice. · Owner Isao Shimabukuro makes the demi-glace, tartar sauce and curry roux from scratch and refuses to cut corners, saying he simply wants delicious food to make people smile. · The flagship 'Daidai Hunton Rice' (around 2,000 yen) is a fluffy omurice crowned with fried white fish, tartar sauce and two oversized shrimp fries; the tartar sauce hides a note of daidai (bitter orange) - the citrus that gives the shop its name - for a refreshing finish. The other pillar is Kanazawa-style cutlet curry (around 1,400 yen), a thick, spiced dark roux over a crisp breaded cutlet and shredded cabbage, served on the classic stainless boat dish.
places.gfd: Not gluten-free friendly. The entire menu centers on wheat-based dishes: Kanazawa curry uses a flour-thickened roux served over a breaded (panko) cutlet, and the Hunton rice is topped with deep-fried breaded white fish and breaded shrimp. places.chef: Matsushita Motohisa · chef-owner, family-run by brothers · Kanazawa, Ishikawa · Founded more than four decades ago, Matsuyoshi is a kappo tucked onto Daikumachi, a quiet side street one block back from busy Katamachi and within walking distance of Korinbo and the Omicho market. places.vgd: A seafood-forward Kaga cuisine restaurant; signature dishes include grilled fish, snow crab, and jibuni (a meat/poultry stew). Dashi is fish/kombu based. No vegan or vegetarian menu is documented.

places.chef: Family-run market stall, Eel and loach charcoal grill, Crab and seafood specialist · Kanazawa, Ishikawa — Omicho Market · Kawaki Shoten is one of the long-standing crab-and-eel specialists in Kanazawa's Omicho Market, run as a family business (有限会社 川木商店). places.chef: onigiri stand, takeaway, market food · Kanazawa, Ishikawa · Musubi is a handmade rice ball (omusubi) shop that has been making onigiri in Kanazawa for over 20 years. Its main store sits inside JR Kanazawa Station, and this smaller branch stands right at the lively entrance of Omicho Market, the city's centuries-old fresh-food market. · The shop's motto, '真心むすびます' (rolled with heartfelt sincerity), reflects its craft approach: rice is cooked over strong gas heat with soft water and washed by hand, then each ball is shaped gently by a craftsperson's hands alone, never with a mold. · Hand-shaped onigiri made from rice specially chosen for rice balls, alongside croquettes (including a Noto-beef heart-shaped croquette) and gold-leaf soft-serve ice cream that nods to Kanazawa's famous gold leaf.

places.chef: soba shop, onigiri specialist · Kanazawa · むすびそば opened in April 2025 on the 2nd floor of かなざわはこまち, a shopping complex about a one-minute walk from the historic Omicho Market in central Kanazawa. places.chef: confectioner, Kaga-fu maker · Kanazawa, Higashi Chaya district · Fumuro Chaya is the tea-house and sweets outpost of Fumuroya (不室屋), one of Kanazawa's most storied makers of Kaga-fu (wheat gluten). The family traces its origin to Fumuro village; Kyuemon settled in Owari-cho (today's main shop) and his heir Rokuemon began making fu around February of Keio 1 (1865), naming the house 'Fumuroya' after the founding village. For over 150 years the company has carried on Edo-period techniques for traditional Kaga-fu — including its famous sudare-fu — while developing new products, and this Higashi Chaya shop lets visitors taste that craft as fresh-gluten sweets in a restored townhouse with a tatami room, veranda, and Kanazawa gold-leaf decoration. · A place to rest and savor a single, refined traditional sweet while strolling the historic tea streets — the shop frames itself as a quiet pause in the middle of sightseeing. · Shira-tama namafu (しら玉生麩) — chewy, mochi-like fresh wheat-gluten dumplings served with a choice of anko (red bean), kinako (roasted soybean flour), or mitarashi (sweet-savory) sauce; plus seasonal namafu sweets such as chilled namafu zenzai in summer and hot kinako-and…

places.chef: Takahiro Hirame · founder, owner · Kanazawa, Ishikawa, Japan · Hiramipan was founded in March 2011 in Kanazawa's Nagamachi district, along the willow-lined Seseragi-dori canal walk. The shop occupies a renovated Taisho-era ironworks (鉄工所跡) wrapped in climbing ivy, with vintage and antique furnishings inside that give it a storybook, Studio-Ghibli-like atmosphere. Founder Takahiro Hirame grew the brand over the years and incorporated it as Hiramipan Co., Ltd. in September 2017, later expanding into related ventures including a creperie, gallery and pizza venue. · The team explicitly resists being 'just an ordinary bakery,' treating bread and pastry as a medium for personal vision and design — comparable to how an illustrator uses a picture book or a designer uses clothing — and aiming to avoid generic, 'tacky' bread. · House-baked bread (croissants, melon pan, scones, canelés including the local 金澤カヌレ) and vegetable-rich morning sets — the croque madame set with homemade chicken ham, bechamel and cheddar topped with a fried egg is the signature, alongside quiche and avocado toast sets; lunch plates pair French bistro fare with salad, carrot rape and ratatouille.

places.chef: owner-chef · Kanazawa, Ishikawa · An independent curry specialist in central Kanazawa. The owner spent more than 15 years researching curry, including time overseas (such as Canada), before realizing a long-held dream of opening the shop around 2015. The result is a personal, ingredient-driven take on Kanazawa curry. · Food that is delicious and makes the body feel good — gently made, light on the stomach, and accessible to people of every dietary style. The shop frames itself as offering 'the most Kanazawa-like Kanazawa curry in the world' with a spirit of omotenashi (hospitality). · A refined Kanazawa-style curry made, by the shop's own description, with no sugar and no wheat flour and seasoned with 27 spices. places.chef: ryotei, kaiseki, Kaga cuisine, historic establishment, wedding venue · Kanazawa (Teramachi, near Nomachi and the Saigawa river), Ishikawa Prefecture, Japan · Tsubajin is Kanazawa's oldest ryotei, founded in 1752 (Horeki 2). Its roots go back further: the Tsuba family served the Maeda clan of Kaga as hereditary tsuba (sword-guard) craftsmen from the late 16th century (the founder entered Kanazawa in 1583 as an armourer to Maeda Toshiie), and the third-generation Jinbei opened a small teahouse called Tsubaya alongside that trade, which grew into the restaurant known today as Tsubajin. The house has carried its craft of Kaga cuisine for roughly 260 years on its present footing as a restaurant. · The house describes its enduring aim across some 350 years as flavors that satisfy and a heart that thinks of the guest, served entirely in private rooms. · Kaga regional cuisine served as kaiseki: signature dishes include jibu-ni (the representative Kanazawa stew), tai no karamushi (sea bream stuffed and steamed), hasu/renmushi (steamed lotus dishes), and a celebrated crab rice porridge (kani-gayu) breakfast. Courses use fresh local seafood and Kaga vegetables.
places.gfd: This is a traditional Kaga kaiseki ryotei built around wheat-based soy sauce, bonito/kombu dashi, and dishes like jibu-ni (which uses flour-dusted meat/fish) and tai no karamushi. There is no documented gluten-free menu, dedicated fryer, or celiac accommodation. Not safe for celiacs. A formal multi-course kaiseki cannot reasonably be made gluten-free here without prior arrangement, and no such accommodation is documented.
places.vgd: A 1752-founded ryotei specializing in Kaga cuisine built on fresh seafood (crab porridge, tai no karamushi, sashimi) and dashi-based dishes. Nothing vegan or vegetarian is documented on the official site or other sources. places.chef: 吉川政史 (Yoshikawa Masashi) · owner-chef, family-run · Ishibiki, Kanazawa · Founded in 1935 (Showa 10), Wakaba is one of the great old-school Kanazawa oden houses, tucked away in the residential Ishibiki neighborhood east of Kenrokuen rather than in the tourist quarters. It is run today by third-generation owner Yoshikawa Masashi, working alongside his father, the second-generation proprietor. · Rather than chasing the modern 'Kanazawa oden' boom, the family deliberately keeps everything the same — their stated ethos is that they have never changed and never will, and that constancy is exactly why regulars keep coming back across generations. · Hand-made iwashi (sardine) tsumire — blended with onion and ginger, said to almost dissolve in the mouth while keeping a characteristic texture, and drinking up the broth; dote-yaki, simmered pork belly crowned with sweet white miso and a heap of minced green onion; plus Kanazawa classics like daikon, taro, octopus and bay snails. Everything bathes in a clear, lightly seasoned dashi built on a niboshi (dried sardine) base that has been continuously topped up since the shop opened.
places.gfd: A traditional oden house built on a continuously replenished dried-sardine dashi seasoned in Japanese style; soy sauce (wheat-based) and miso are central, and items like tsumire and dote-yaki are not gluten-free. No gluten-free accommodation is documented. Not celiac-safe.
places.vgd: The entire menu rests on a fish (niboshi/sardine) dashi, and signature dishes include sardine tsumire, pork-belly dote-yaki, octopus and bay snails. There are a few plant-based oden items (daikon, taro, konnyaku, grilled tofu) but they are all simmered in the fish broth, so the place is not suitable for vegans.

places.chef: 田尻綾子 (Ayako Tajiri) · owner, baker · Kanazawa, Ishikawa · COYA. is a small bakery in the Oyama-cho neighborhood beside Oyama Shrine, run single-handedly by baker Ayako Tajiri. Its plain white-washed facade blends into the retro streetscape around the shrine. A 2019 renovation added a Sunday-only café space on the second floor, where coffee from a Toyama roaster is served alongside café-exclusive breads. · Tajiri puts quality over quantity, baking only as much as she can make well each day and closing once it sells out. In her words she wants to keep making 'unpretentious bread you won't tire of even eating it every day,' letting the natural sweetness of the ingredients come through. · Hard-crust breads are the heart of the shop: a raisin-and-currant loaf, a Dainagon sweet-red-bean stick, and a chocolate baguette (choco-france). The house pain de mie comes in three styles — plain, sesame, and walnut — and draws daily regulars. The most talked-about item is the lemon cake, a French-style pound cake folded with lemon juice.
places.gfd: This is a wheat-flour bakery; bread is the entire product line. No gluten-free items, dedicated equipment, or allergy accommodations are documented. Not suitable for celiac or gluten-avoidant diners.
places.vgd: A few of the signature items lean plant-forward — hard breads such as the raisin/currant loaf and Dainagon (red bean) stick may be made without dairy or egg — but the bakery also sells dairy/egg-rich goods (lemon cake, scones, cookies) and publishes no vegan labeling. Vegans would need to ask about each item; nothing is confirmed.

places.chef: owner-bakers (the Wakai couple) · Kanazawa, Japan · Shintate Bake Store opened on April 12, 2023, in the Shintatemachi shopping street as the sister shop of the much-loved Kanazawa bakery Sakanoue Bakery (坂の上ベーカリー), run by the Wakai couple. In September 2023 the original Sakanoue Bakery closed and its bread workshop moved here, making Shintate Bake Store the continuation of that bakery's craft. · The theme is 'healthy and delicious' (健やかで美味しく) — bread and sweets made with ingredients gentle on children, adults, and the environment, using pesticide-free organic wheat that is milled in-house and natural yeast. The owners deliberately do not serve coffee in the shop, encouraging customers to wander the shopping street and pair their bread with a drink from a neighboring cafe. · More than 20 kinds of bread and pastries are laid out daily from around 9 a.m., centered on breads made from home-milled organic whole wheat. Signature items include the Fukumitsuya canelé made with rice shochu from the local Fukumitsuya sake brewery, and the playful 'SS Cherry Pie' (a Twin Peaks reference, where SS stands for Shintate Street).
places.gfd: This is a wheat bakery — its entire identity is bread made from home-milled organic wheat and whole wheat flour. There is no gluten-free offering and it is not safe for celiacs.
places.vgd: No documented vegan labeling. Breads use natural yeast and organic wheat; some items (canelé, cherry pie, pastries) clearly contain dairy/eggs. Simple lean breads may be plant-based but this is not confirmed, so vegans should ask about specific loaves.

places.chef: Yoshimura Ryoichiro · chef, owner · Kanazawa, Ishikawa (Daikumachi, Katamachi area) · Founded in 1977 in Kanazawa's Daikumachi quarter, a small street historically lined with kappo restaurants near the Saigawa river. places.gfd: Not gluten-free friendly. This is a traditional Kaga kappo built on soy sauce and dashi, and the signature jibu-ni is thickened and includes fresh wheat gluten (sudare-fu/fu). No gluten-free menu or dedicated handling is documented; not safe for celiacs.
places.vgd: Not vegan-friendly. The menu is centered on Sea of Japan seafood (sashimi, sweet shrimp, nodoguro, snow crab) and meat (duck in jibu-ni), with dashi-based seasoning throughout. No vegan options are documented.

places.chef: 石黒格 (Ishiguro Itaru) · owner, group founder · Kanazawa, Ishikawa — a homegrown offshoot of the city's Itaru izakaya group. · A specialty shop devoted almost entirely to one dish — nodoguro-meshi, a bowl of premium blackthroat seaperch. places.chef: 茶店 (teahouse), 甘味処 (sweets house), 加賀料理 (Kaga cuisine restaurant), souvenir/craft shop · Kanazawa, Ishikawa — within the grounds of the Special Place of Scenic Beauty, Kenrokuen Garden. · Tsutsumitei was founded in 1888 (Meiji 21) and occupies a building more than a century old on the historic tea-shop street of Kenrokuen, one of Japan's three great landscape gardens. With its calm, russet-walled rooms and second-floor tatami chambers overlooking the garden, it has served generations of visitors near the Katsurazaka entrance and Kanazawa Castle's Ishikawa Gate. · A traditional teahouse experience: enjoy regional Kaga cuisine and Japanese sweets in a historic garden setting, with veranda seating for a quick matcha and dango or upstairs rooms for a full meal. · Kanazawa's signature Kaga dish jibu-ni (a stew of duck/meat and vegetables), served on its own or as jibu-ni udon and soba; also a sweet-shrimp rice bowl. places.gfd: Not gluten-free friendly. The signature dishes are jibu-ni (a stew thickened with wheat flour and seasoned with wheat-based soy sauce), plus udon and soba, all containing wheat. places.chef: chef trained in Kyoto, family/independent garden teahouse operator · Kanazawa, inside Kenrokuen Garden · Kenrokutei occupies one of the most enviable addresses in Kanazawa: inside Kenrokuen Garden, looking out over what is said to be Japan's oldest fountain. The kitchen is led by a chef who trained at a well-regarded Kyoto establishment, and the place leans on that pedigree while staying rooted in Kaga's own food culture. · The cooking emphasizes handmade, additive-free dishes built on seasonal local vegetables and seafood, served in a calm room with garden views. · The house specialty is an original "jibu soba" — the classic Kaga dish jibu-ni reimagined over noodles, with crisp roasted chicken and Kaga renkon (lotus root) worked into the soba. places.gfd: Not gluten-free friendly. Soy-based dashi and seasonings are used throughout. No gluten-free menu or accommodations are documented. Celiac travelers should not consider this safe.
places.vgd: Not a vegan destination. The cooking centers on chicken, seafood (sea urchin, nodoguro, sushi), Noto beef, and dashi stock. No vegan or vegetarian set menus are documented. A vegan diner could potentially ask about the cafe (sweets, matcha lattes, local teas), but wagashi and dairy lattes are not reliably plant-based and nothing is confirmed. Best to treat as ask-only with very limited prospects.

places.chef: Heritage Kaga-ryori ryotei, Custodian of Maeda-clan culinary tradition, Maker of historic Kanazawa railway bento · Kanazawa (Kaga domain) · Otomoro is a long-established Kanazawa ryotei founded in 1830 (Tenpo 1), whose family long served as cooks to the Maeda lords of the Kaga domain. places.notes: A long-running Kanazawa washoku restaurant, established in 1971, set near the Nagamachi samurai district just off Korinbo. Over more than half a century it has built its reputation on Kaga regional cooking and the seafood of the Sea of Japan.
places.chef: Kaga local cuisine, seafood washoku, crab specialist · Kanazawa, Ishikawa · A long-running Kanazawa washoku restaurant, established in 1971, set near the Nagamachi samurai district just off Korinbo. Over more than half a century it has built its reputation on Kaga regional cooking and the seafood of the Sea of Japan. · The kitchen keeps preparation as simple as possible to let the natural flavor of carefully sourced ingredients come through (素材本来の味を生かす為、調理はできるだけシンプルにして), aiming to make refined Kanazawa cuisine approachable. · Nodoguro (blackthroat seaperch, grilled or as sashimi), Ishikawa snow/Kano crab, natural rock oysters, white gas shrimp sashimi, the house crab-cream croquette, and Kaga local dishes including jibuni (duck simmered in soy-seasoned broth). Seasonal lineup spans firefly squid and gas shrimp in spring, rock oysters and Kaga vegetables in summer, hairy crab and sweet shrimp in autumn, and Kano crab and winter yellowtail in winter.

places.chef: Shiro Shintani (新谷 志郎) · chef-owner · Born in Ishikawa Prefecture in 1994 · Shintani grew up around cooking — his father was a professional chef and his siblings also went into the trade — and he entered the kitchen himself at age 15. He trained in hotels and traditional ryokan and worked his way up to head chef at the popular Katamachi izakaya 'Sho' before going independent and opening Shokudo Tsuki in April 2022. He is a certified sake sommelier (kikisake-shi). · The name 食道 ('the path of food') reflects his wish to roam freely across genres rather than be boxed into formal washoku, balancing respect for tradition with playful creativity. He wants guests to drop in casually and spend a relaxed, unfussy evening. · Daily-changing seasonal Japanese cooking driven by what he hand-picks at the market each morning, with fresh fish at the heart of the menu. Signature plates include seasonal sashimi (季節の鮮魚のお造り), a chilled simmered-anago bowl, grilled yanagi-sawara finished with sudachi, and a raw Hokkaido (Nemuro) uni hand roll that regulars have followed him from his 'Sho' days as a favorite closing dish. He pairs these with local sake sourced from across Japan.

places.chef: fishmonger, grilled-seafood counter operated by Ohguchi Suisan · Kanazawa, Ishikawa — inside Omichō Market · The Yakiyaki Corner is the grilled-seafood standing counter of Ohguchi Suisan, one of the largest and longest-running fishmongers in Kanazawa's roughly 300-year-old Omichō Market, with one of the market's biggest sales floors. Alongside its fresh-fish cases, the shop runs an open grill where market-fresh seafood is skewered and cooked right in front of customers to eat on the spot. · The shop leans on ingredients pulled straight from the market's own fish counters, aiming for affordable, market-fresh seafood eaten casually on the spot. · Charcoal-grilled skewers from about 200 yen each — squid legs, scallops, salt-grilled nodoguro (blackthroat seaperch), eel liver, Noto-region fugu and shrimp — plus fresh sashimi and sushi packs (sushi offered on Sundays and holidays), often washed down with a 350-yen draft beer.

places.chef: Igarashi · owner-chef · Kanazawa, Ishikawa · The chef behind this small Seseragi-dori counter spent nine years training at the celebrated Asadaya ryotei in Kanazawa, then served nine more years as head chef at Lamp no Yado in Suzu, the famed seaside ryokan on the Noto Peninsula, before opening his own place in May 2014. · He cooks for contrast and season — temperature, flavor and texture, seasonality, and the cleverness of combinations — and deliberately keeps prices approachable so that this level of craft stays within reach. · Seasonal Kaga kaiseki built on local seafood and Kaga vegetables, served as fixed omakase courses — refined cooking that plays with temperature, texture, and seasonal pairings.
places.gfd: This is a traditional Kaga kaiseki/kappo kitchen built around dashi, soy sauce, and seasonal seafood — all of which involve wheat-based seasonings (regular soy sauce contains wheat). There is no gluten-free menu and no documented allergen handling. Not suitable for celiacs.
places.vgd: A seafood- and Kaga-vegetable-focused seasonal kaiseki restaurant serving fixed omakase courses. Fish, dashi (typically bonito/kombu), and animal products are central to every course; there is no vegan menu and dishes cannot meaningfully be made vegan. Not a vegan destination.

places.chef: owner, master · Kanazawa · Tucked down a lane in the 柿木畠 (Kakinokibatake) quarter just off Katamachi — reached by crossing a small bridge over the Kurazuki canal, near the 21st Century Museum — Hickory opened in 1988 as 珈琲 ヒッコリー. The owner first took over his father's dry-cleaning shop on this spot before converting it into a coffee house a few years later. In its early years it filled with students, when Kanazawa University still occupied the nearby castle grounds (until 1995). · The owner, a former smoker, deliberately made the cafe non-smoking so families would feel welcome. There is no Wi-Fi, no power outlets and no BGM — it is a quiet, unhurried room built for coffee and conversation. · A Showa-retro kissaten known for siphon-brewed coffee, curry topped with a soft omelette (curry omurice), parfaits, cheese toast and a hazelnut coffee. Its most personal dish is 太洋軒の焼きめし, a nostalgic fried rice the owner revived from the long-closed local restaurant Taiyoken, a recipe passed to him by Taiyoken's son — 'only I can make it,' he says.
places.gfd: A Showa-era kissaten whose signature dishes are curry omurice, fried rice, cheese toast and parfaits — wheat-based bread, roux, and flour are central to the menu. No gluten-free accommodation is documented and the kitchen is a single owner-run operation. Not suitable for celiacs.
places.vgd: The menu centers on egg-topped curry, omelette-based dishes, butter chicken curry, cheese toast, and dairy-rich parfaits and coffee drinks. No vegan options are documented. Animal products (egg, dairy, meat) are core to nearly every dish.

places.chef: 乙部 友寿 (Otobe Tomohisa) · head chef / owner · Born in Ishikawa Prefecture in 1974 · Sushidokoro Asanogawa opened in the summer of 2016 in Kanazawa's Kazuemachi teahouse district, on a quiet lane beside the Asano River near Omicho Market. Its name was bestowed by Morita Kazuo, the revered sushi master who ran the celebrated 'Komatsu Yasuke,' and the shop carries on his techniques. Chef Otobe Tomohisa, born in 1974, grew up in a restaurant family, went to Kyoto after high school to train in Japanese cuisine at ryotei-ryokan for four years, then returned to Kanazawa to deepen his knowledge of local seafood — before inheriting Morita's secret methods when Komatsu Yasuke closed. · 妥協しない技で寿司に向き合い、心を込めておもてなし致します — to face the sushi with uncompromising technique and serve with wholehearted hospitality. · Counter omakase sushi built on carefully selected fish, with Ishikawa coastal catch such as nodoguro (rosy seabass); a marinated red-tuna (maguro no akami-zuke) preparation carries the mark of the Komatsu Yasuke lineage.
places.gfd: This is a traditional sushi house. Sushi is served with wheat-based soy sauce, and nimono/marinades and dashi typically contain soy sauce and other wheat-containing seasonings. No gluten-free menu or celiac protocol is documented. Not suitable for celiac diners.
