places.chef: Fujii Makoto (藤井誠) · owner, chef, soba master · Owner-chef Fujii Makoto trained for more than a decade in Nagano and Tokyo, including time in the Edo soba tradition, before opening his own shop in 1999 - an era when dedicated soba specialists were still rare in Kanazawa. The restaurant moved from its original Katamachi location to the quiet Kakinokibatake lane behind the 21st Century Museum of Art in March 2011, settling into a calm, machiya-like townhouse space. · Fujii treats raw material as everything - 'ingredients are the lifeblood of soba' - and travels each year to meet his buckwheat producers in person, sourcing directly rather than settling for what is convenient. · Hand-cut soba in several styles - the everyday nihachi (80% buckwheat) zaru, a coarse-ground (arabiki) version, a 100% buckwheat juwari, and the elegant pale 'sarashina' (gozen) soba made from highly refined buckwheat, prized for its clean throat-feel and delicate aroma. Alongside the noodles, Fujii serves refined small plates such as roast duck, scallop-filled tamagoyaki, vegetable tempura, oysters and salted sea urchin, all meant to pair with sake or buckwheat shochu.
places.gfd: Not gluten-free safe. The house standard is nihachi soba (80% buckwheat, 20% wheat flour), and the signature pale "sarashina" soba uses refined buckwheat but is still made in a wheat-handling kitchen. A 100% buckwheat (juwari) soba appears on the menu, but it is prepared in the same kitchen alongside wheat-bound noodles, so cross-contamination is essentially certain. Dipping sauces (tsuyu) and many side dishes also use wheat-based soy sauce. Celiac travelers should avoid.
places.vgd: Not a vegan destination. The dipping broth is bonito-dashi based, and the menu leans on duck, scallop, sea urchin and oysters. Plain noodles and vegetable tempura exist but most accompaniments are not vegan; ask before ordering.

places.chef: 佐野 陽平 (Yohei Sano) · owner, chef · Kanazawa, Japan · Genzaemon sits in Kiguramachi, a Kanazawa dining quarter with over 300 years of history. The restaurant takes its name from Genzaemon Sano, said to be a Kamakura-era samurai whose descendants carried on a tradition of hospitality — including, by the house's telling, once entertaining a shogun of the day. Owner Yohei Sano runs the house in a traditional farmhouse-style (kominka) setting, with counter seats that look out onto Kaga Yuzen textiles. · Owner Sano describes his consistent approach as responding to things from the customer's point of view, pairing local fish and Kaga vegetables with a deep selection of Hokuriku and nationwide sake (around 100 varieties). · Sashimi and dishes built around fresh fish delivered from Kanazawa Port (nodoguro/blackthroat seaperch is a highlight), Kaga regional cooking using Kaga vegetables, Noto beef sukiyaki, and a signature lotus-root dumpling in dashi broth that combines grated lotus root with mountain yam for a fluffy, chewy texture. A hidden specialty is hoba miso yaki (miso grilled on a magnolia leaf) using beef or seasonal items like scallop and firefly squid.
places.gfd: This is a Kaga regional cuisine and local-fish kappo where dashi, soy sauce, miso (hoba miso), tempura, and sake-based seasonings are central to nearly every dish. There is no documented gluten-free menu or allergen accommodation, and the kitchen relies heavily on wheat-containing soy sauce and miso. Not safe for celiacs.
places.vgd: The restaurant is built around fresh fish from Kanazawa Port (sashimi, nodoguro, etc.), Noto beef sukiyaki, and dashi-based regional dishes. While Kaga vegetable dishes exist (e.g., Kaga thick cucumber, lotus-root dumplings), they are prepared with fish/bonito dashi and are not vegan. No vegan menu is documented.

places.chef: 中川 清一 (Nakagawa Seiichi) · chef-owner · Opened 2008 in the riverside teahouse quarter near Omicho Market, in a quiet building whose second-floor window seats look out over the Asano River and whose first-floor tables face a small inner garden (tsuboniwa). · Chef-owner Nakagawa Seiichi trained at a Kanazawa hotel and at creative-Japanese and kappo restaurants in the city before opening Kifune in 2008 in the Kazue-machi/Hikoso teahouse district along the Asano River. · Nakagawa caps service at four groups per seating so that every dish can be prepared and timed perfectly for each table — an expression of his ideal of offering 'the finest hospitality possible today' while keeping the essence of traditional Japanese cuisine approachable across ages and cultures. · Monthly-changing seasonal kaiseki that turns over on the 15th of each month, with winter highlights of crab and white fish, beautifully composed multi-course meals, and a celebrated Sunday-only 'Kanazawa asage' breakfast where rice is cooked tableside in individual clay pots using premium Ishikawa rice.
places.gfd: Traditional Kaga kaiseki built on dashi and Japanese soy sauce, with no documented gluten-free menu, dedicated equipment, or allergen handling. Wheat-containing soy sauce is integral to this style of cuisine, so it should not be considered celiac-safe.
places.vgd: Course menus are seafood- and fish-dashi-centered (sashimi, scallop/squid salads, white fish and crab in winter, beef hot pot at the Sunday breakfast). places.chef: 北出美由紀 (Kitade Miyuki) · owner, cook · 東京出身（金沢へ移住） · Mamezuki was opened in 2016 by Kitade Miyuki and her husband Kitade Takesuke (北出健展), a first-class architect, who relocated to Kanazawa from Oiso in Kanagawa. Searching for a traditional Japanese way of living, they were drawn to Kanazawa's active machiya-preservation scene and fell for an 80-plus-year-old townhouse in the Higashiyama district, which Takesuke renovated by hand while preserving its courtyard garden, tea room, and alcove. · The couple cook at 'the pace of the beans' — black beans are simmered slowly over roughly three days, never with a pressure cooker — and live by a motto of doing things 'within their means' (身の丈に合っている), honoring local culture and preparing each dish with care. The shop typically keeps around 15 varieties of beans on hand and serves them in ceramics by regional and national artisans. · Beans are the whole story. places.chef: family-run lacquerware house (Nosaku, est. 1780) · Kanazawa, Ishikawa · Urushi no Mi is the tea room on the 4th floor of Nosaku, a Kanazawa lacquerware house founded in 1780 that has carried on Kaga maki-e and Wajima lacquer traditions for more than two centuries. The cafe opened over twenty years ago, conceived as a quiet, elegant salon — the kind you might find tucked inside a luxury boutique — where guests rest with a sweet after browsing the lacquerware below. · The room is built around savoring the seasons of Kanazawa — cherry blossoms, fresh greenery, autumn color and snow seen from the windows over Hirosaka — paired with refined, traditional Japanese sweets in a hushed, unhurried setting. · Matcha cream zenzai (matcha cream over mochi dumplings and sweet red beans) and made-to-order matcha kuzukiri are the signature offerings, alongside high-grade Yoshihashi wagashi served with matcha. places.chef: independent neighborhood cafe · Kanazawa (Nishi Chayagai / Nomachi) · Yusura is a cafe set inside a traditional Kanazawa machiya townhouse in the atmospheric Nishi Chayagai geisha district, a short walk from Nomachi Station. The building previously housed a sushi restaurant; it reopened as a cafe in the wave of interest that followed the Hokuriku Shinkansen reaching Kanazawa in 2015. places.gfd: Not gluten-free friendly. No gluten-free menu or accommodation is documented, and Japanese curry roux and katsu breading both contain wheat. A celiac diner should not consider this a safe option.

places.chef: seafood and Kaga cuisine restaurant, market dining destination · 近江町市場（いちば館2F）, central Kanazawa · Ichi no Kura sits on the second floor of the Ichiba-kan building right inside Omicho Market, the centuries-old marketplace locals call 'Kanazawa's kitchen.' The restaurant draws directly on that bustling market energy, sourcing fish and crab from just downstairs and serving them in a warm, wood-filled dining room. · To let visitors enjoy the lively spirit of Omicho Market over a meal — pairing Kanazawa sightseeing with fresh local seafood — and notably to offer crab dishes all year rather than only in season. · Seafood market cuisine and Kaga regional dishes: seasonal fish set meals and kaisen-don rice bowls at lunch, and at dinner traditional Kaga fare alongside crab served year-round. Signature plates include crab miso grilled in the shell (かに味噌甲羅焼き), crab salad, duck jibuni stew (鴨の治部煮), and squid-liver miso grill (いかわた味噌焼き).
places.gfd: This is a seafood and Kaga-cuisine restaurant built around fish, crab, tempura, grilled dishes, and rice bowls. Cooking relies heavily on Japanese soy sauce, miso, and dashi — all of which typically contain or are processed with wheat — so it cannot be considered celiac-safe. No gluten-free menu, gluten-free soy sauce, or dedicated preparation is documented, and signature dishes (jibuni stew, crab miso shell-grill, set meals) are wheat- and dashi-based. A celiac traveler should not rely on this…
places.vgd: The entire concept is seafood-market cuisine: live crab, seasonal fish, sashimi, rice bowls, and duck jibuni. Dashi (bonito/fish stock) underlies most dishes. No vegan or vegetarian menu is documented and the kitchen is fundamentally fish- and meat-based. Not a viable option for vegans or vegetarians.

places.chef: standing-counter beef stall, market food stop · Kanazawa, Ishikawa (Omicho Market) · A small standing-counter stall tucked into the Omicho Ichiba-kan building on the first floor of Kanazawa's lively Omicho Market, Takumi specializes in Noto beef — a prized local brand. Noto beef is raised in the nature and sea breeze of the Noto Peninsula and is so scarce (only around 930 head shipped a year, almost all consumed within Ishikawa) that locals call it a phantom brand. · Making premium, hard-to-find Noto beef approachable — grilled fresh and eaten immediately, standing right there in the market, so visitors can taste a regional luxury without a formal restaurant. · Seared Noto beef nigiri (aburi sushi) and hand-skewered, grilled Noto beef. The kitchen sources A5-grade-or-higher Noto beef, skewers each stick by hand, and grills to order. For the seared nigiri it uses Ishikawa Koshihikari rice, lightly torches the surface of the beef, and finishes it with the shop's own soy-based sauce. The lineup also includes seared tuna and seared gunkan rolls.
places.gfd: Not gluten-free. The seared nigiri and skewers are served with the shop's own soy-based sauce (Japanese soy sauce normally contains wheat), and rice/sushi is central. No gluten-free menu, no dedicated handling, and no allergen information published. Not suitable for celiacs.
places.vgd: Not vegan. This is a dedicated Noto beef stall — every menu item (seared beef nigiri, beef skewers, seared beef rolls) centers on A5-grade beef. There are no plant-based options.
places.hours: 10:00–16:00 (per Omicho Market official listing). Tabelog lists Fri–Sun 09:00–16:00, closed Mon–Thu. Effectively a weekend-focused operation; weekends can see lines and early sell-outs.

places.gfd: A traditional fruit parlor serving parfaits with cake, cookies, cereal/granola and wheat-based components; no gluten-free menu or celiac handling is documented, so it is not safe for celiacs.

places.chef: family-run fermented-food maker, cafe operator · Kanazawa (Yayoi district, near the Teramachi temple area south of the Sai River) · Shijimaya Honpo was founded in 1875 (Meiji 8) and has spent roughly 150 years making Kanazawa's traditional fermented foods, most famously kaburazushi (turnip cured with yellowtail and rice koji) and daikon-zushi. The Yayoi main store occupies a Kanazawa machiya (townhouse) building that has kept its traditional appearance for about 140 years, in an area recognized for its preserved historic streetscape. · The company frames its work around valuing local tradition and contributing to healthy, enriched living through food and fermentation. · In one renovated section of the historic shop the family opened a 'fermentation cafe,' turning the koji expertise behind their pickles into gentle, body-friendly sweets and drinks: amazake (sweet rice-koji drink), amazake soda in flavors such as shiso, yuzu and ginger, and koji-based gelato including amazake and amazake-yuzu-basil.

places.chef: 矢田 紀彦 (Norihiko Yada), founder; with son 佳弘 (Yoshihiro) and grandson 勇紀 (Yuki) · family-run, three-generation, owner-operated · Kanazawa, Ishikawa (小立野 / Komatsuno) · Founded in 1967 (Showa 42) by Norihiko Yada, who had trained at Kanazawa Western-style eateries including Grill Tanuki Chaya and borrowed the kanji 狸 (tanuki) from his old employer as a tribute when he opened his own place. places.gfd: This is a classic yoshoku kitchen built on wheat — demi-glace, fried cutlets (panko), gratin and soy-seasoned fried rice all feature heavily, and the demi-glace base is simmered for about a week. places.chef: barista, pastry chef · Kanazawa · This is the second location of Sunny Bell Coffee, a self-roasting specialty coffee shop regarded as one of Kanazawa's representative coffee houses, whose flagship sits in Kasaichi-machi. The Owaricho branch opened on April 17 (2024), tucked between the Higashi Chaya geisha district and Omicho Market. · Where the flagship is a coffee-first counter, the Owaricho location was conceived as a place to slow down: its stated concept is for guests to relax and savor sweets and drinks at leisure, and the dessert lineup was broadened accordingly. · Self-roasted drip coffee and graceful latte art carry over from the original shop, but this branch leans into sweets: a tiramisu panna cotta with espresso-soaked biscuit and mascarpone-cream cheese, seasonal mini panna cotta parfaits (mango, blueberry), and house soft serve ice cream (with an affogato option).
places.gfd: Not a gluten-free destination. The signature desserts (tiramisu/panna cotta with biscuit, macarons) and the general café context mean wheat is present. No gluten-free handling or dedicated preparation is documented, so this is not celiac-safe; plain black coffee is naturally GF.

No vegan menu or plant-milk options are documented. A black drip coffee or espresso would be the only incidental vegan order; ask about milk alternatives, as none are confirmed.

places.chef: Masashi Takamatsu (高松雅志) · owner, roaster, barista · Kanazawa, Ishikawa · Sunny Bell Coffee is the flagship roastery of Masashi Takamatsu, an award-winning latte artist who has placed in multiple latte-art competitions. He opened the shop in 2013 and moved it to its current Kasaichi-machi premises in 2017, building a five-seat space where vintage roasting equipment is on full view to customers. · Takamatsu emphasizes the individual characteristics of each bean, monitoring color and aroma closely to preserve fragrance and aims to deliver a special cup that is hard to reproduce at home. · House-roasted single-origin specialty coffee (typically 5-7 varieties on offer) brewed by meticulous hand pour, alongside signature sweets such as canelé and tiramisu. He roasts on a Fuji Royal R-105 semi-hot-air 5kg roaster, favoring light-to-medium roasts that highlight each bean's individual character.
places.gfd: A specialty coffee stand, not a gluten-free destination. The food offerings are wheat-based pastries such as canelé and tiramisu, and no gluten-free menu or celiac-safe handling is documented. Black coffee and the bean selection are naturally gluten-free, but there is no dedicated GF preparation, so it is not suitable for strict celiacs beyond plain coffee.
places.vgd: Not a vegan venue. The signature sweets (tiramisu, soft-serve, pudding, parfaits) are dairy- and egg-based, and milk-based lattes feature heavily. Black drip coffee and whole-bean purchases are plant-based, but no plant-milk option or vegan food is documented; a vegan visitor would need to ask and would largely be limited to black coffee.

places.chef: second-generation owner-proprietor · Kanazawa, Ishikawa · Founded in 1996, this neighborhood soba shop sits near Wakamiya Bridge in the Futakuchi-machi district on the station-west side of Kanazawa. It is now run by the second-generation proprietor, who carries forward the traditions inherited from the founder while applying, in the shop's own words, 'old wisdom with new thinking.' · The shop describes itself as 'a place to enjoy soba and sake together' (蕎麦と日本酒を楽しむ場), emphasizing painstaking effort and quality ingredients. · The house specialty is coarsely-ground nine-tenths buckwheat soba (粗挽き九割そば) with a rich, rustic flavor and a distinctive texture, served with a dashi built on bonito, Rishiri kombu and dried shiitake. The most famous dishes are the tenmori (soba with lightly fried shrimp and seasonal vegetables) and a premium oyakodon made with charcoal-grilled chicken and rich 'Ranoh' (蘭王) red eggs from Oita Prefecture over a house dashi-based sauce.
places.gfd: This is a buckwheat soba shop, but the signature noodle is described as "九割そば" (nine-tenths buckwheat), meaning roughly 10% wheat flour binder is used — so the soba itself is NOT gluten-free. The dashi-based broths (soba tsuyu, oyakodon sauce) are made with kombu and bonito but typically also contain wheat-based soy sauce/mirin. There is no documented gluten-free menu, no dedicated preparation, and no allergy protocol on the official site or any fetched source. Not safe for celiac diners.
places.vgd: A traditional soba and izakaya-style shop. Broths are built on bonito (katsuo) and kombu dashi, and signature dishes feature charcoal-grilled chicken and eggs (oyakodon, tenmori with fried shrimp). No documented vegan menu or plant-based options. Not suitable for vegans; a vegan would need to ask, and even plain soba is served with fish-based dashi tsuyu.

places.chef: owner-operator · Kanazawa · A long-running Showa-retro junkissa (pure coffeehouse) tucked into a residential pocket of Honcho, about a five-minute walk from Kanazawa Station behind the hotel district. It has been in operation for over 30 years; the Honcho shop is actually the second location, the original having stood near what is now Musashi's studio street. The building predates the cafe itself and was reinforced with sturdy pillars to keep it standing. · Preserves an increasingly rare junkissa culture: an unhurried, understated space for savoring a cup of coffee, the kind of place that would be nearly impossible to recreate today. · A clean, refreshing blend coffee well suited to a quiet morning, alongside classic kissaten fare like toast and lunch sets, plus nostalgic touches such as a sprinkle-topped coffee float.
places.gfd: This is a classic Showa-era Japanese coffeehouse (junkissa) whose menu centers on toast, sandwiches and lunch sets built on bread, plus coffee. The core offerings are wheat-based and there is no indication of gluten-free preparation or any allergen accommodation. Not suitable for celiacs or strict gluten avoidance.

places.chef: 鷹 秀徳（たか ひでのり） · owner · 金沢・尾張町 · The café sits inside Gallery Mita, the former Mita drapery shop (旧三田商店) — a reinforced-concrete building raised in 1930 (Showa 5) with scratch-tile walls and Art Deco detailing, designated a National Registered Tangible Cultural Property in 1997 and counted among the finest surviving modern buildings in Kanazawa. places.gfd: A Showa-era kissaten serving cakes, curry and hayashi rice — all wheat-based — with no documented gluten-free menu, dedicated fryer, or allergy accommodation. Coffee and plain hot drinks are the only items unlikely to contain gluten, but cross-contamination cannot be ruled out and staff allergy handling is undocumented.
places.vgd: No vegan offering is documented. The menu centers on coffee/tea, cakes (fruit cake, granola cheesecake — contain dairy/egg) and light meals like curry and hayashi rice. places.chef: seafood izakaya, oden specialist, market eatery · Kanazawa (Omicho Market) · A compact market eatery on the second floor of the Omicho Ichiba building, right inside Kanazawa's famous Omicho fresh-food market near Musashigatsuji. The shop brings the market's catch straight upstairs, pairing it with the city's beloved oden in one casual spot built for both locals on a lunch break and visitors exploring the market. · Freshness and local sourcing first: fish bought direct from the surrounding market, Noto-grown rice, and regional sake and ingredients combined so visitors can taste several Kanazawa specialties in one small space. · Kanazawa oden served alongside market-fresh seafood: sashimi and seafood rice bowls (including a nodoguro/throat-perch don), sushi, and Noto beef dishes such as a grilled Noto-beef rice bowl, with rice from Noto Koshihikari and local Hokuriku sake to match.
places.gfd: Not celiac-safe and no gluten-free menu is documented. Kanazawa oden is built on a fish/dashi broth simmered with wheat-containing fish cakes (練り物) and seasoned with regular (wheat-based) soy sauce, and the kitchen also serves sushi, tempura-style and grilled rice-bowl dishes, so cross-contact is unavoidable. Celiac travelers should avoid; others with mild sensitivity should ask staff directly.
places.vgd: No vegan or vegetarian offering. The menu is centered on fresh seafood (sashimi, nodoguro and seafood rice bowls, sushi), Noto beef, and Kanazawa oden made with fish-based dashi and seafood/meat ingredients. No plant-based dish is documented; vegans cannot eat here in a meaningful way.

places.chef: family-run, owner-operated · Noto Island (能登島), Ishikawa — Enome harbor · 鮨 えのめ is a small family-run sushi counter tucked inside Kanazawa's lively Omicho Market. Its defining feature is a direct line to the sea: the owner's family are fishermen (網元, amimoto — heads of a fishing operation) at Enome harbor on Noto Island, and the catch is delivered fresh each morning straight from that family operation, supplemented by direct buying at Kanazawa Port. · Direct sourcing from the family's own Enome fishing harbor and Kanazawa Port, served casually so visitors can enjoy top-grade local seafood amid the open, energetic atmosphere of the market. · Its signature is a seafood rice bowl (海鮮丼) heaped with eleven kinds of seasonal fish and shellfish, alongside sushi featuring sea urchin (uni), salmon roe (ikura) and seared nodoguro (blackthroat seaperch). There is no documented gluten-free menu, no dedicated preparation area, and no indication of celiac-safe practices. Not suitable for celiacs.
places.vgd: The entire concept is fresh fish and shellfish delivered daily from the family's fishing operation on Noto Island — seafood rice bowls, sushi, sea urchin, salmon roe, crab and nodoguro. There are no documented vegan dishes; this is not a destination for plant-based diners.

places.chef: Kaoru Fukue (福江 薫) · owner, cook · Kanazawa, Japan · Aka is a retro kissaten hidden up a small staircase between a butcher and a rice-ball shop near the Emza entrance of Omicho Market. The owner, Kaoru Fukue, opened it here about four decades ago despite having no prior ties to the market; he was simply drawn to the room's unusual trapezoidal shape. Though it sits in one of Kanazawa's busiest tourist areas, most of the regulars are people who work in the market. · The menu grew organically out of listening to customers. As Fukue puts it, the shop originally served little more than fried udon and sandwiches, but expanded over time in response to regulars saying what they wanted to eat. · Drip coffee is the heart of the place, alongside its much-loved homemade baked curry (yaki-curry). Over the years the kitchen has added light meals like jako (dried-fish) fried rice, sandwiches and spaghetti.

places.chef: owner · 海鮮つるや is a seafood-bowl restaurant inside Kanazawa's Omicho Market, the centuries-old food market locals call 'Kanazawa's kitchen.' A relative newcomer, it opened around 2022 and quickly became a popular stop for fresh kaisendon. It is sized deliberately large for the market so guests can be seated quickly: '極力待たせないように、と80席のキャパシティで客を迎えている' (the place welcomes guests with 80 seats so as to keep waiting to a minimum). · A commitment to Kanazawa's local flavors paired with quick, comfortable seating that suits everyone from solo diners at the counter to larger groups. · Seafood rice bowls are the draw, from the lavish 特上海鮮丼 piled with nodoguro (blackthroat seaperch), tuna, white shrimp, salmon roe, octopus, sea bream, sweet shrimp, squid, salmon, crab claw and steamed shrimp, to the value おまかせ市場丼. Signature single-topping bowls include the のど黒丼 (nodoguro bowl), いくら丼 (salmon roe bowl) and かんぱち丼 (amberjack bowl). Beyond bowls, the kitchen leans into local Kanazawa flavors with 金沢おでん simmered in a well-developed bonito broth, regional sake from local breweries, and northern delicacies such as Noto sea mozuku and Toyama firefly squid in oil pickle.
places.gfd: This is a seafood-bowl and Kanazawa-oden restaurant where wheat-based soy sauce, dashi, and other seasonings are central; nothing in the sources indicates gluten-free accommodation or awareness, so it is not suitable for celiacs.
places.vgd: The restaurant is built around raw fish, seafood bowls, and dashi-based dishes. places.chef: seafood-bowl and Kanazawa oden eatery, market food stop with local sake · Kanazawa, inside Omicho Market (上近江町) · When the long-loved Jimonotei seafood-bowl shop inside Omicho Market closed at the end of 2024 after years in business, it didn't simply disappear. places.chef: Kaga-cuisine kappo, dining restaurant within a culinary ryokan · Kanazawa (Honmachi, near the station east exit) · Kappo Tsuzumi is the dining heart of Kanazawa Chaya, a culinary ryokan in the Kagaya hospitality group, a short walk from the east exit of Kanazawa Station. places.chef: 宮村宏志 (Miyamura Hiroshi) · owner, kabayaki maker · Kanazawa, Ishikawa — Omicho Market · 金沢近江町市場 みやむら is a small family-run shop (about five people) in Kanazawa's Omicho Market specializing in charcoal-grilled kabayaki. In Kanazawa, 'kabayaki' traditionally means loach (dojou) rather than eel, a local delicacy at its best from roughly May to July, and Miyamura is one of a handful of kabayaki vendors keeping that culture alive in the market. Owner Miyamura Hiroshi and his family do everything by hand — buying live fish, making their own tare, and grilling over charcoal in-house. · Everything is made in-house from live fish to sauce, using natural salt and purified water. The shop puts flavor above cheap pricing — its master's stated commitment is to fillet the river fish that same morning, since the oils fade once the fish is cut, and to have customers leave wanting to come back to Miyamura. · Charcoal-grilled loach kabayaki (dojou no kabayaki) — the Kanazawa signature — using 100% domestic wild loach, plus freshwater eel (unagi) kabayaki filleted from live fish each morning (Miyamura says it is the only shop in Omicho Market that fillets its eel in-house). places.n: 金茶寮 本店 (Kincharyo Honten)
places.notes: Kincharyo opened in 1933 (Showa 8), taking over the villa of Baron Yokoyama, a former chief retainer of the Maeda family who ruled the million-koku Kaga domain. places.chef: fu maker, restaurant · Kanazawa (Higashiyama / Higashi Chaya area) · Suzuan is the restaurant arm of Kaga Fuzukasa Miyata, a long-established Kanazawa fu (wheat gluten) maker founded in 1875 (Meiji 8). Set in a quiet residential pocket within walking distance of the Higashi Chaya District, the dining room has a traditional wooden interior, a view onto a courtyard garden, and distinctive lapis-lazuli-toned walls. · To carry forward the heritage of Kaga fu — a craft refined in the Edo period by Funaki Den'nai, a chef to the ruling Maeda clan, who perfected fu that would not fall apart when simmered (the 'sudare-fu' used in jibuni) — while also demonstrating that fu can pair with Western ingredients and modern techniques. · Multi-course fu cuisine that shows off the versatility of 麩 — raw fu (生麩) served sashimi-style, glazed and fried fu, fu 'steak', vinegared and simmered preparations, and fu-based sweets finished with black honey, alongside the Kaga classic 治部煮 (jibuni). places.chef: restaurant · Kanazawa Kagami opened in 2019 as the oden-kaiseki sister restaurant of Amatsubo, a long-established Kaga regional-cuisine and izakaya group founded in 1964 with more than half a century of history in the city. It occupies a renovated roughly hundred-year-old machiya (traditional Kanazawa townhouse) a short walk from Kanazawa Station, where aged wooden beams and traditional architecture are paired with a calm, modern interior. · The restaurant works from the idea of 食の温故知新 — drawing on tradition while evolving it — so that guests can taste both the heritage and the modern evolution of Kanazawa oden in a single meal. · The signature is 'oden kaiseki' — Kanazawa oden reimagined and served course-style, plate by plate, with different broths matched to individual ingredients. The multi-course oden kaiseki showcases seasonal local produce sourced from nearby markets such as Omicho, alongside seasonal seafood, and an extensive list of Ishikawa sake (including Kuroobi, Tengu Mai, and Gorin).
places.gfd: Not gluten-free safe. This is a Kanazawa oden kaiseki restaurant where dishes are simmered in dashi-based broths and seasoned with soy sauce, which in Japan almost always contains wheat. There is no documentation of gluten-free accommodation, dedicated equipment, or wheat-free options. A celiac traveler should not consider this restaurant safe.
places.vgd: Not suitable for vegans or vegetarians. The cuisine centers on Kanazawa oden and Kaga regional kaiseki built around bonito/kombu dashi, seafood (including items such as hotaruika/firefly squid and seasonal fish), and animal-based ingredients. No vegan or vegetarian course is documented. A plant-based diner could at best ask, but the menu is fundamentally fish- and dashi-based.

places.chef: 山田寿人 (Yamada Hisato) · owner-chef · Ryomon is a machiya (traditional townhouse) bistro tucked one street behind the main thoroughfare of Kanazawa's Higashi Chaya geisha district, where it blends seamlessly into the historic teahouse streetscape. places.chef: Kakura · owner · Kanazawa · Kado no Mise occupies the spot of 'Shima' (島), a beloved okonomiyaki shop that ran for roughly 50 years and served as an after-school hangout for neighborhood kids in the 1960s-70s before closing for over a decade following its elderly owner's passing. Owner Kakura used to come here as a schoolboy, buying simple okonomiyaki for around 15 yen and cooking it himself on the griddle. After a 2016 alumni reunion at the nearby elementary school, talk turned to the shuttered shop; when the building came up for sale, Kakura bought it and reopened it as Kado no Mise, recreating Shima's recipes with help from the original owner's daughter and her suppliers. · Kakura, a former company head who once trained at a German hotel school and dreamed of opening a bakery, runs the place as 'doraku' (a labor of love / hobby) rather than a serious business, and has declined offers to expand so the shop stays small and manageable. The name 'corner shop' happens to echo the German 'An der Ecke' (at the corner) he once imagined for that bakery. · Yakisoba served the old-school way in a donburi bowl eaten with a fork (inherited from Shima), griddle okonomiyaki (from about 220 ye…
places.gfd: Wheat is central to the entire menu — okonomiyaki batter, yakisoba noodles, takoyaki, and taiyaki are all wheat-flour based and finished with wheat-based sauces. This is not a celiac-safe environment and there is no documented gluten-free handling.

places.chef: owner · A casual yet refined kappo-style seafood izakaya in Kanazawa's Katamachi entertainment district, set in a restored traditional wooden building with gunjo (indigo) walls — a historically prestigious Kanazawa color — and decorative candy molds. The ground floor has an open kitchen with counter seating so guests can watch the chefs work, while upper floors offer private tatami rooms. · The house motto is '大衆の値、割烹の味' — people's prices with kappo-quality cooking — built on locally sourced seafood and regional ingredients from the sea and mountains of Hokuriku. · Nodoguro (rosy seabass), called 'the king of white fish' for its rich, melting fat: served as seared sashimi, grilled, and as seared nodoguro sushi. Also known for abundant 'bucket' sashimi platters of seafood landed that morning, and Kanazawa oden simmered in Noto ishiru (fish sauce), with more than 15 local Ishikawa sake varieties.
places.gfd: A seafood izakaya built around soy-sauce and dashi-heavy Japanese cooking. Signature dishes like sashimi, seared nodoguro and grilled nodoguro sushi rely on soy sauce (wheat), and the Kanazawa oden is simmered in ishiru (fish sauce) and includes wheat gluten (fu). There is no documented gluten-free menu, dedicated fryer, or allergen handling. Not suitable for celiac diners.
places.vgd: This is a fish- and seafood-centered kappo/izakaya — nodoguro, sashimi platters, smoked mackerel, and oden simmered in fish sauce (ishiru) are the core of the menu. places.chef: owner-family, fishmonger · Nanao City, Noto region (founding family) · Run by the Kawabata family, who hail from Nanao in the Noto region. The Katamachi flagship opened in 2009 in Kanazawa's main entertainment district, with a later branch added in Kikuracho around the time of the Hokuriku Shinkansen's arrival. Rather than a polished seafood restaurant, it deliberately adopts a working fishmonger aesthetic — fishing gear, flags and sake-brewery aprons decorate the room, staff dress in fishmonger uniforms, and display cases and tanks of live fish and shellfish greet you at the entrance. · Bring the freshness and value of a fish market straight to the table — sourcing whole tuna and catch delivered fresh from Ishikawa's fishing ports, and letting diners grill it themselves over charcoal. · Five-piece sashimi platters of regional catch, shichirin (tabletop charcoal) grilling of fresh fish and shellfish, buri-shabu (yellowtail hot pot), and seasonal items such as natural Noto rock oysters in summer; paired with local sake.
places.gfd: This is a wheat- and soy-sauce-heavy seafood izakaya with no documented gluten-free accommodation. Sashimi and grilled fish are served with regular soy sauce (which contains wheat), and tempura/fried items and izakaya sauces are common. Not safe for celiacs without bringing your own tamari and confirming each dish; no dedicated GF handling is documented.
places.vgd: A seafood-focused izakaya built around fresh fish, shellfish, sashimi and charcoal grilling; dashi (bonito/fish stock) is pervasive. There is no documented vegan menu or vegan-friendly preparation. Not a suitable destination for vegans.

places.chef: sake retailer, the only liquor shop in Omicho Market · Omicho Market, Kanazawa · Sake no Ozawa has stood inside Omicho Market - long called the kitchen of Kanazawa - for more than a hundred years, and it is the only liquor merchant within the market. places.chef: Tachinomiya Co. (operator) · Kanazawa (Honmachi), part of the locally founded Tachinomiya / Daisho family of standing bars · A friendly standing-bar gyoza joint about a seven-minute walk from Kanazawa Station, in the Honmachi neighborhood. It belongs to a homegrown Kanazawa company, Tachinomiya Co., which began in 2009 with a skewer bar called Kushi Sakaba Daisho; the founder, Masayuki Higo, fell in love with Osaka's standing-bar culture during an apprenticeship there and brought that easygoing, shoulder-to-shoulder spirit back home. The gyoza shop is one of several 'Daisho' standing bars the group runs around the city. · The parent company sums up its outlook as keeping smiles alive on both sides of the noren — a town where everyone can smile equally. The shop itself is built on the simple idea that gyoza and beer make the ultimate 'golden combo' to enjoy casually. · Hand-made gyoza is the headliner, with seven-plus varieties on offer: the signature 大笑餃子, griddle-fried with a crisp finish and a note of star anise; a coriander/pakuchi gyoza with the herb worked into the filling; and a garlic-heavy stamina gyoza. Fried rice, ramen and simple izakaya small plates round out the menu.
places.gfd: The whole concept is gyoza (wheat-flour dumpling wrappers) plus Chinese small plates and Chinese-style oden, almost certainly cooked with wheat-based soy sauce. There is no gluten-free menu and the kitchen is built around wheat — not safe for celiacs.
places.vgd: A meat-and-drink standing bar: gyoza, stamina gyoza, Chinese oden and izakaya snacks are the draw, typically pork/meat-filled and made with soy/meat-based seasonings. No vegan menu is documented; not a fit for vegans.

places.n: Conconto Kashiten (コンコント菓子店)
places.notes: [GF-dedicated] A rare 100% wheat-free patisserie in Kanazawa: all cakes, tarts, Mont Blanc and parfaits are built from rice flour and beans, with no wheat, buckwheat or peanut anywhere in the kitchen. This is one of the safest cafe stops in the region for celiacs, and it doubles as a plant-based cafe (soy-milk ice cream, custard). Sit-in seating (~8 seats) means you can enjoy a parfait or cake with Kaga bōcha tea on the spot.
places.chef: Koji Yamazaki (山崎弘二) · owner, founder · Kanazawa, Ishikawa, Japan · Yamazaki worked in Western pastry manufacturing and production management before handling sales for his family's Kaga lacquerware wholesale house (山崎又一商店). places.n: Kamuna (しぜんおやつ工房カムナ)
places.notes: [GF] Rice-flour natural-sweets shop, NOT celiac-safe as-is: the owner deliberately bakes spelt (古代小麦) on some Sundays in the same tiny kitchen and publishes no cross-contact controls. Products also contain egg and butter (not vegan). If visiting, avoid Sundays, and message @kamuna357 or LINE beforehand to confirm the day's items are wheat-free and how equipment is handled. places.chef: owner, maker · Kanazawa, Ishikawa, Japan · The owner is a former nurse (元看護師) and mother who started Kamuna during the pandemic (opened Jan 11, 2022) out of a preventive-medicine conviction — wanting healthy snacks she would feel good feeding her own children, priced so kids can buy them with their own pocket money. She cites rising childhood allergies, mental illness and cancer as part of what drove her, and uses pesticide-free Ishikawa rice flour (無農薬米粉), mochi flour, Ishikawa free-range eggs, and no white sugar (muscovado and organic maple instead) with no additives. · Affordable, additive-free, mostly rice-flour 'natural sweets' for children's health — while keeping 'a relationship with wheat as an occasional indulgence' (「時々食べる嗜好品として小麦とお付き合いしていきます」), with spelt (ancient-wheat) scones and bread on occasional Sunday 'wheat gratitude' days. · カムナどらやき — dorayaki pairing a moist shiratamako (glutinous rice-flour) skin with a sugar-free koji-fermented anko; plus sesame brownies/pound cakes, sablé butter sandwiches and rice-flour tarts.

places.notes: [GF-dedicated] The whole kaffee-konditorei Y / Petit pas kitchen is wheat-free - all bread is 100% 山田錦 rice flour and all cakes are wheat-flour-free, run by celiac owners. places.n: タイル (TILE)
places.notes: Experience restaurant where you pick toppings from ~30 ingredients for your own kaisendon. Vegetarian "Kanazawa Mosaic" shōjin bowl (¥3,300): paprika, takuan, cucumber, mixed beans, shiitake, oboro kelp, micro greens, myoga. Entry by door code through a nijiriguchi. Listed by kanazawa-food.jp (Egg/dairy free, Wheat free, Vegetarian, Vegan).
